bathroom-waterproofing.q: What is the average cost to waterproof a bathroom?
bathroom-waterproofing.a: In Australia, waterproofing a standard bathroom costs $500–$1,200 in labour plus materials. The membrane, primer, bond breaker and reinforcing bandage together run roughly $250–$450 at retail. Expect more for large wet areas, upstairs bathrooms, or remedial work over existing tiles.

bathroom-waterproofing.q: Can I waterproof a bathroom myself?
bathroom-waterproofing.a: In Queensland waterproofing must be done by a licensed waterproofer, and in most other states it needs to meet AS 3740 and be certified for insurance and resale purposes. Since most bathroom leaks trace back to failed DIY membranes, a certificate from a licensed tradie is usually worth the labour cost.

blocked-drain-repair.q: How much does it cost to clear a blocked drain in Australia?
blocked-drain-repair.a: Most blocked drains cost $150–$500 to clear. A simple machine-cleared blockage sits at the low end; high-pressure water jetting with a CCTV camera inspection typically runs $300–$600. After-hours emergency callouts add $100–$250 to the bill.

blocked-drain-repair.q: How do plumbers clear blocked drains?
blocked-drain-repair.a: Plumbers use an electric eel (drain snake) or a high-pressure water jetter, then a CCTV drain camera to find the cause. In Australia the most common culprit is tree roots entering older clay or terracotta sewer pipes at the joints. Which is why blockages tend to come back if only cleared, not repaired.

blocked-drain-repair.q: Can I unblock a drain myself?
blocked-drain-repair.a: A plunger or hand auger is worth trying on a slow sink or shower. But recurring blockages, gurgling from multiple fixtures, or sewage smells point to a main-line problem that needs a licensed plumber. Avoid caustic chemical cleaners. They damage older pipes and make the eventual professional job messier.

hot-water-system-installation.q: How much does a new hot water system cost installed?
hot-water-system-installation.a: Installed prices in Australia typically run $1,200–$2,500 for electric storage, $1,500–$3,000 for gas continuous flow, and $2,500–$5,500 for a heat pump before government rebates. The unit itself is $500–$2,000 at retail, with labour, valves and compliance making up the rest.

hot-water-system-installation.q: How long does it take to install a hot water system?
hot-water-system-installation.a: A like-for-like replacement takes a licensed plumber 2–4 hours. Switching fuel types (electric to gas or heat pump), relocating the unit, or upgrading tempering valves and switchboard circuits can stretch the job to a full day.

hot-water-system-installation.q: Should I repair or replace my hot water system?
hot-water-system-installation.a: Storage systems last 8–12 years. A leak from the tank itself means replacement: the cylinder has corroded through. Faulty valves, elements or thermostats are repairable for $150–$400, but on a unit near the 10-year mark that money is usually better put toward a new system.

switchboard-upgrade.q: How much does a new electrical switchboard cost?
switchboard-upgrade.a: A switchboard upgrade costs $800–$2,000 in most Australian homes, including a new enclosure and RCBO safety switches on every circuit. Asbestos backing-panel removal, meter relocation, or consumer mains upgrades can push a complex job to $3,000+.

switchboard-upgrade.q: Do I need to upgrade my switchboard?
switchboard-upgrade.a: Yes if your board still has ceramic fuses, lacks safety switches, or trips regularly. An upgrade is usually required when adding solar, an EV charger, or a major appliance circuit. Insurers and electricians treat old fuse boards as a fire risk, and safety switches are mandatory on new circuits under current wiring rules.

switchboard-upgrade.q: How long does a switchboard upgrade take?
switchboard-upgrade.a: Most upgrades take half a day, with power off for 2–4 hours while the electrician swaps the board and tests every circuit. Jobs involving asbestos panels or defective consumer mains need a second trade or the distributor involved and can run across two visits.

safety-switch-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a safety switch?
safety-switch-installation.a: Installing a safety switch (RCD/RCBO) costs $150–$350 per circuit in Australia, including the device and an electrician's labour. Protecting a whole house during a switchboard upgrade is more economical than doing circuits one at a time.

safety-switch-installation.q: Are safety switches mandatory in Australia?
safety-switch-installation.a: Yes. Current wiring rules require RCD protection on new and altered circuits nationwide, and Queensland requires safety switches on all circuits when a property is sold or rented. Older homes are often only protected on power points, leaving lights, ovens and air conditioners uncovered.

safety-switch-installation.q: What is the difference between a safety switch and a circuit breaker?
safety-switch-installation.a: A circuit breaker protects the wiring: it trips on overload or short circuit. A safety switch protects people: it detects current leaking to earth (through a person, for example) and cuts power in about 30 milliseconds. Modern RCBOs combine both in one device.

gyprock-installation.q: Is Gyprock the same as plasterboard?
gyprock-installation.a: Yes. Gyprock is CSR's brand of plasterboard, the way Americans say drywall. Standard 10mm sheets retail for roughly $11–$41 depending on size and grade, with wet-area, soundproof and fire-rated variants costing more.

Modern plasterboard contains no asbestos. The risk in Australian homes built before 1990 is older fibro (asbestos cement) wall and ceiling sheeting that looks similar to plasterboard. If your home predates 1990, get suspect sheeting tested before sanding, cutting or demolition.

gyprock-installation.q: How much does gyprock installation cost?
gyprock-installation.a: Supplied, fixed and flush-jointed, plasterboard installation costs about $40–$60 per square metre in Australia. The sheets themselves are only $11–$41 each. Most of the price is the setting and sanding labour that determines whether walls look flat under paint.

colorbond-roof-installation.q: How much does a Colorbond roof cost in Australia?
colorbond-roof-installation.a: A full Colorbond roof replacement on an average Australian home costs $18,000–$35,000, or roughly $50–$95 per square metre supplied and installed including removal of the old roof. Corrugated sheet itself retails around $20–$40 per lineal metre.

colorbond-roof-installation.q: Is Colorbond actually made in Australia?
colorbond-roof-installation.a: Yes. Colorbond steel is made by BlueScope at Port Kembla, NSW, and has been used on Australian roofs for over 50 years. That local manufacture is why it carries bushfire (BAL) ratings and warranties matched to Australian conditions.

colorbond-roof-installation.q: Is a Colorbond roof better than tiles?
colorbond-roof-installation.a: Colorbond is lighter (allowing smaller framing), sheds rain faster at low pitches, and performs well in bushfire zones. Tiles win on sound insulation and individual-tile repairability. Most re-roofing in Australia now goes tile-to-Colorbond rather than the reverse.

concrete-driveway-installation.q: How much does a concrete driveway cost in Australia?
concrete-driveway-installation.a: Plain concrete driveways cost $65–$110 per square metre installed in Australia; exposed aggregate runs $100–$150 and coloured or stamped finishes sit between. A typical double driveway (35–45m²) lands at $2,500–$6,000 including excavation and mesh.

concrete-driveway-installation.q: How much will 20kg of concrete cover?
concrete-driveway-installation.a: A 20kg bag of concrete mix ($9–$14 at retail) yields about 10 litres. Enough for 0.1 of a square metre at 100mm slab thickness. That is why driveways use premixed truck concrete: a single cubic metre replaces roughly 100 bags.

concrete-driveway-installation.q: What is the 4 2 1 rule for concrete?
concrete-driveway-installation.a: It is the classic site mix ratio: four parts gravel, two parts sand, one part cement. For structural work like driveways, though, Australian contractors order batched N25–N32 concrete from a plant, because backyard mixing cannot guarantee consistent strength across a slab.

timber-paling-fence-installation.q: How much does a timber paling fence cost?
timber-paling-fence-installation.a: Treated pine paling fences cost $75–$120 per metre installed in Australia, so a typical 20m boundary run is $1,500–$2,400. Materials are roughly 13 palings per metre at $3–$6 each, plus posts every 2.4m, two or three rails per bay, and concrete for footings.

timber-paling-fence-installation.q: What does H4 and H3 mean in timber?
timber-paling-fence-installation.a: They are hazard treatment levels. H3-treated timber suits outdoor use above ground. Palings and rails. H4 is treated for in-ground contact, which is why fence posts must be H4: an H3 post set in soil will rot at the ground line years early.

timber-paling-fence-installation.q: What is the best timber for outdoor use in Australia?
timber-paling-fence-installation.a: Treated pine is the standard for fencing: cheap, straight and termite-resistant. For decking and screens where looks matter, merbau and spotted gum are the common upgrades. Whatever the species, the treatment level (H3 above ground, H4 in ground) matters more than the timber name.

interior-painting.q: How much does it cost to paint a house interior in Australia?
interior-painting.a: Painting a three-bedroom home's interior costs $2,500–$7,000 in Australia, or roughly $10–$30 per square metre of wall including two coats. Quality interior paint retails at $75–$200 per 10L, and a 10L drum covers about 50–60m² with two coats.

interior-painting.q: What paint finish should I use on interior walls?
interior-painting.a: Low-sheen is the Australian default for walls. Washable without highlighting imperfections. Use flat/ceiling white overhead, and semi-gloss on trims, doors and wet-area woodwork. Save full gloss for feature joinery, since it shows every brush mark and wall defect.

interior-painting.q: How many coats of paint does an interior wall need?
interior-painting.a: Two topcoats is the standard, over an undercoat if you are changing colour dramatically or painting new plasterboard. One-coat claims rarely survive scrutiny in real light. The second coat is what gives even colour and a washable film.

exterior-painting.q: How much does exterior house painting cost in Australia?
exterior-painting.a: Exterior painting costs $8,000–$20,000 for a typical three-bedroom Australian home, or $15–$45 per square metre depending on height, access and surface condition. Exterior acrylic retails around $80–$200 per 10L, but preparation labour is the real cost driver.

exterior-painting.q: How often should you repaint a house exterior?
exterior-painting.a: Every 7–10 years for quality acrylic on weatherboard or render in Australian conditions. Sooner on harsh coastal or full-sun western elevations. Chalking, hairline cracking and fading colour are the signs the film has stopped protecting the substrate.

exterior-painting.q: What is the best time of year to paint a house exterior?
exterior-painting.a: Autumn and spring: mild temperatures, lower humidity and no overnight dew sitting on fresh film. Avoid painting in direct summer sun (paint skins too fast and shows lap marks) and winter mornings where surfaces stay damp past 10am.

carpet-laying.q: How much should a carpet cost?
carpet-laying.a: Carpet supplied and laid with underlay costs $40–$90 per square metre in Australia, so a 12m² bedroom runs $500–$1,100 and a full three-bedroom home lands around $5,000–$10,000. Budget carpet alone retails from about $7 per square metre before underlay and fitting labour are added.

carpet-laying.q: Is it cheaper to lay flooring or carpet?
carpet-laying.a: Carpet is usually cheaper upfront: budget carpet supplied and laid starts around $40 per square metre versus $60–$100 for laminate or hybrid flooring. Hard flooring costs more initially but lasts longer and skips the replacement carpet needs every 8–10 years in high traffic areas, so it depends on your time frame.

carpet-laying.q: What is the cheapest carpet you can buy?
carpet-laying.a: Budget polypropylene loop-pile carpet is the cheapest option, retailing from about $7–$13 per square metre before underlay and installation. It holds up fine in bedrooms and low traffic areas but wears faster than nylon or wool blends. Underlay and fitting typically double the total cost per square metre.

cornice-installation.q: What is the purpose of a cornice?
cornice-installation.a: Cornice covers and seals the join between wall and ceiling, hiding gaps and shrinkage cracks for a finished look. Cove cornice (90mm) costs about $14–$24 per 4.8m length in Australia, plus adhesive. Installed cost including labour runs $8–$15 per linear metre for a standard cove profile.

cornice-installation.q: What is the difference between a cornice and a coving?
cornice-installation.a: In Australia the terms are used interchangeably for the moulded strip covering the wall-ceiling join. Coving usually means that curved shape specifically, while cornice can also cover square-set, bullnose or decorative profiles. Decorative styles cost more than the standard $14–$24 per 4.8m cove length.

cornice-installation.q: What is the difference between a cornice and an architrave?
cornice-installation.a: Cornice sits at the wall-ceiling join, while architrave frames doors and windows where the wall meets the timber. Both are finishing trims but cover different junctions. Cove cornice costs roughly $14–$24 per 4.8m length, with architrave priced separately by the metre depending on profile and timber species.

merbau-decking-installation.a: Yes, merbau is a popular hardwood decking choice in Australia: naturally durable, termite resistant and needs no chemical treatment. Boards retail from about $8–$15 per linear metre. It does leach red tannins in the first few rains, which wash onto surrounding paving, so hose the deck down after installation.

No, merbau is imported from Southeast Asia and the Pacific, mainly Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Malaysia. It's sold widely through Australian timber yards and hardware stores from about $8–$15 per linear metre. Local alternatives with similar durability include spotted gum and ironbark, both grown and milled in Australia.

Merbau costs more than treated pine because it's a slow-growing imported hardwood with natural termite and rot resistance, needing no chemical treatment. Expect $8–$15 per linear metre for boards versus $4–$7 for treated pine decking. Supply has also tightened as sustainably certified merbau gets harder to source.

villaboard-installation.q: Is Villaboard the same as cement sheeting?
villaboard-installation.a: Yes. Villaboard is James Hardie's branded fibre cement sheet, the same product category as generic cement sheeting or compressed sheet. A 6mm sheet retails for roughly $45–$70 in Australia. It's rated for wet areas like bathrooms and laundries, unlike standard plasterboard, which breaks down when it gets wet.

villaboard-installation.q: Do you screw or nail Villaboard?
villaboard-installation.a: Screw it. Villaboard is fixed with corrosion resistant screws at 200mm centres on sheet edges and 300mm through the field, never nails, since nails back out over time and fibre cement is too dense for a clean nail fix. A 6mm sheet costs roughly $45–$70 before fixings and jointing compound.

villaboard-installation.q: Do I need to waterproof a Villaboard?
villaboard-installation.a: Yes, in shower and bath areas. Villaboard is water resistant, not waterproof. AS 3740 requires a membrane over the sheet joints and penetrations in wet areas before tiling. Skipping the membrane on Villaboard alone is one of the most common causes of bathroom leaks in Australian renovations.

caesarstone-benchtop-installation.q: Is Caesarstone still legal in Australia?
caesarstone-benchtop-installation.a: Engineered stone was banned from 1 July 2024 due to the silicosis risk from cutting it, but Caesarstone benchtops already installed remain completely legal and safe once in place. New engineered stone benchtops can no longer be manufactured, supplied or installed here, so kitchens now use porcelain, laminate or natural stone instead.

Caesarstone is an engineered quartz product, roughly 90 percent crushed quartz bound with polymer resin and pigment. It was popular for benchtops at $400–$900 per linear metre installed before Australia's 2024 ban on engineered stone. Porcelain benchtops are now the closest legal replacement at a similar price point.

Caesarstone (engineered stone) was more stain and scratch resistant than natural marble and needed no sealing, but it's no longer available new in Australia after the 2024 engineered stone ban. Marble remains legal, costs $500–$1,500+ per linear metre installed, and needs periodic sealing to resist etching from acidic foods.

rangehood-installation.q: Which type of rangehood is best?
rangehood-installation.a: Ducted rangehoods are best because they actually remove cooking odours and moisture, venting outside rather than recirculating air through a filter. A 600mm rangehood retails for $65–$135 in Australia. Recirculating models are cheaper to install but only filter grease, not steam or smell, from the kitchen air.

rangehood-installation.q: Does a rangehood need to be vented outside?
rangehood-installation.a: Not legally, but it performs far better if it is. Ducted rangehoods vent steam, heat and cooking smells outside; recirculating models just filter grease through charcoal and return the air to the kitchen. Ducting adds installation cost but is worth it, especially in enclosed kitchens with poor cross ventilation.

rangehood-installation.q: Do you legally need a rangehood in Australia?
rangehood-installation.a: There's no single blanket law, but Australian plumbing and building codes generally require mechanical ventilation above a cooktop, and a rangehood is the standard way to meet that. Councils and certifiers check for it at renovation approval. A 600mm rangehood costs $65–$135 supplied, before installation and ducting.

whirlybird-installation.a: Yes, in the right roof. A wind driven whirlybird extracts hot air from the roof cavity, noticeably dropping summer roof space temperatures and easing pressure on air conditioning. They cost $80–$220 supplied in Australia. They work best on larger roofs and do little without matching intake vents at the eaves.

whirlybird-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a whirlybird?
whirlybird-installation.a: A whirlybird costs $80–$220 for the unit, plus $150–$350 in labour for a licensed roofer to cut in and flash it properly. Total installed cost typically lands at $250–$500 per unit in Australia, more on steep or multi-storey roofs needing extra access equipment.

A whirlybird is a wind driven turbine vent that spins with any breeze to pull hot, moist air out of the roof cavity. This lowers roof space temperature in summer and cuts condensation risk in winter. Units cost $80–$220 supplied, with most homes fitted with one per 50–90m² of roof.

colorbond-fencing-installation.q: How much does COLORBOND cost per metre?
colorbond-fencing-installation.a: Colorbond fencing costs $70–$150 per linear metre supplied and installed in Australia, depending on fence height, ground conditions and how many gates or corners are needed. A standard 1.8m back yard fence sits toward the lower end, while colour matched capping and taller pool-compliant panels push the price up.

colorbond-fencing-installation.q: Is COLORBOND actually made in Australia?
colorbond-fencing-installation.a: Yes. Colorbond steel is manufactured by BlueScope at Port Kembla, NSW, and has been used across Australian roofing and fencing for over 50 years. That local production is why it carries corrosion and colour warranties matched to Australian climate zones, from tropical Queensland to salty coastal exposure.

Colorbond steel is stronger, cheaper and better for full privacy fencing at $70–$150 per linear metre installed. Aluminium slat fencing costs more, often $300–$700 per panel, but resists denting and never rusts, making it the better pick for coastal properties or a more open, architectural look.

concrete-slab-for-shed.q: How much will 20kg of concrete cover?
concrete-slab-for-shed.a: A 20kg bag of premixed concrete ($9–$14 at retail) covers about 0.1 square metre at 100mm thickness, or roughly 10 litres of wet mix. For a shed slab you need batched truck concrete instead: a typical 3x3m base at 100mm thick needs about 0.9 cubic metres, equal to roughly 90 bags.

concrete-slab-for-shed.q: What is the 4 2 1 rule for concrete?
concrete-slab-for-shed.a: It's the classic hand-mix ratio: four parts gravel, two parts sand, one part cement. That's fine for small footings but not a shed slab, since backyard mixing can't guarantee consistent strength across the pour. Shed slabs should use batched N20–N25 concrete ordered from a plant and reinforced with mesh.

concrete-slab-for-shed.q: Is concrete the same as cement?
concrete-slab-for-shed.a: No. Cement is the powder binder, about $9–$15 per 20kg bag, that mixed with sand, gravel and water becomes concrete. A shed slab is concrete, not cement: for a typical 3x3m base you'd order around 0.9 cubic metres of batched concrete rather than hand-mixing individual bags.

travertine-paving.a: Travertine sits in the mid-to-premium bracket: pavers retail for about $50–$100 per square metre, with supply and lay installed cost around $100–$180 per square metre in Australia. It costs more than concrete or clay pavers but less than premium granite or marble paving.

travertine-paving.q: What are the disadvantages of travertine?
travertine-paving.a: Travertine is porous and needs sealing every 1–2 years to resist staining, especially around pools with chlorine and sunscreen. It can also get slippery when honed smooth, so a tumbled or brushed finish is safer outdoors. Budget $100–$180 per square metre installed, plus ongoing sealing costs.

travertine-paving.q: Is travertine out of style in 2026?
travertine-paving.a: No, travertine remains a popular natural stone choice for Australian pool surrounds and courtyards, prized for staying cooler underfoot than porcelain or concrete in direct sun. At $100–$180 per square metre installed it costs more than concrete pavers, but the natural variation and heat performance keep demand steady.

insulation-batts-installation.q: What is the best type of insulation?
insulation-batts-installation.a: For most Australian homes, glasswool or polyester ceiling batts rated R4.0–R6.0 give the best value, costing $50–$100 per pack covering about 10–14 square metres, with no specialist tools needed. Reflective foil suits humid climates and underfloor spaces, while rigid foam boards cost more but rate higher per millimetre.

insulation-batts-installation.q: What is the best insulation for Australian walls?
insulation-batts-installation.a: R2.5 polyester or glasswool batts are standard for external walls across most of Australia, balancing thermal performance with cost. Acoustic batts are worth the upgrade between bedrooms and living areas. Wall batts typically run $40–$80 per pack, and only work well if fitted without gaps or compression around wiring.

insulation-batts-installation.q: What are the rules for insulation in Australia?
insulation-batts-installation.a: The National Construction Code sets minimum ceiling and wall R-values by climate zone, generally R3.5–R6.0 for ceilings and R1.4–R2.8 for walls. Ceiling batts cost $50–$100 per pack. Installers must also keep insulation clear of downlights and exhaust fans unless it's IC-rated, to avoid a fire risk.

turf-laying.q: Can I just lay turf over dirt?
turf-laying.a: No, not directly. Turf needs 50–100mm of quality garden soil or turf underlay spread and levelled first, or the grass won't root properly and low spots will pond water. Sir Walter buffalo turf costs about $10–$19 per square metre supplied, so skipping soil prep to save money usually costs more in dead patches.

turf-laying.q: What time of year should I lay turf?
turf-laying.a: Spring and autumn are best across most of Australia, when soil is warm and rainfall is more reliable for establishing new roots. Turf laid in the middle of summer needs daily watering to survive the heat, and winter growth is too slow to root before frost. Sir Walter runs $10–$19 per square metre.

turf-laying.q: How much does turf cost to lay in Australia?
turf-laying.a: Turf costs $25–$50 per square metre supplied and laid in Australia, depending on grass variety and how much site preparation the yard needs. Sir Walter buffalo runs $10–$19 per square metre for the turf alone (farm direct to retail), and synthetic turf runs $13–$23 per square metre for the product.

acoustic-insulation.q: How much does acoustic insulation cost in Australia?
acoustic-insulation.a: Acoustic insulation costs $10 to $25 per square metre installed in Australia, with acoustic batts themselves running around $75 a pack at retail. Total price depends on wall or ceiling area, batt thickness, and whether plasterboard needs removing and refitting around the new batts. A single internal wall usually sits at the lower end.

acoustic-insulation.q: Does acoustic insulation actually reduce noise?
acoustic-insulation.a: Acoustic insulation does reduce noise, though it will not block sound entirely. Dense glasswool or polyester batts fitted snugly between wall or ceiling studs absorb airborne noise like voices, TVs, and traffic. Pairing batts with acoustic sealant around gaps and resilient mounts on plasterboard improves results further.

acoustic-insulation.q: Where is acoustic insulation most worth installing?
acoustic-insulation.a: Acoustic insulation gives the best return in shared walls between bedrooms, home theatres, laundries, and walls facing busy streets. Ceilings under upstairs living areas also benefit. Installers typically use higher-density batts in these spots than standard thermal insulation, since sound absorption depends more on density than R-value.

bathroom-tap-installation.q: How much does bathroom tap installation cost in Australia?
bathroom-tap-installation.a: Installing a bathroom tap costs $150 to $400 in Australia for a straightforward swap, covering the tap itself ($90 to $325) plus one to two hours of licensed plumber labour at $80 to $200 an hour. Costs rise if old pipework needs replacing or the vanity needs reconfiguring.

bathroom-tap-installation.q: Can I install a bathroom tap myself?
bathroom-tap-installation.a: You can fit a like-for-like tap yourself if you are comfortable with basic plumbing and turn off the water first, but any change to pipe layout or fitting a new mixer legally requires a licensed plumber in Australia. Getting the seal wrong risks leaks inside the vanity or wall.

bathroom-tap-installation.q: How long does a bathroom tap last before it needs replacing?
bathroom-tap-installation.a: A quality mixer tap typically lasts 10 to 15 years before washers, cartridges, or the finish wear out. Cheaper taps may need cartridge replacement within a few years. Signs it is time to replace rather than repair include persistent dripping, stiff handles, and corrosion around the base or spout.

cement-rendering.q: How much does cement rendering cost in Australia?
cement-rendering.a: Cement rendering costs $30 to $80 per square metre installed in Australia, including polymer render mix (around $15 per 20kg bag) and reinforcing mesh (about $51 a roll). A full house elevation adds up quickly, so most homeowners get a per-wall quote rather than costing it bag by bag.

cement-rendering.q: Can you render over old brickwork?
cement-rendering.a: Cement render can go over most brick, block, and besser walls provided the surface is clean, structurally sound, and free of loose paint or efflorescence. Cracked or crumbling brickwork needs repair first, and a bonding agent or mesh is often added to help the new render key in properly.

cement-rendering.q: Does cement render crack over time?
cement-rendering.a: Cement render can develop hairline cracks over time from building movement, poor mixing, or applying coats too thick or too fast. Reinforcing mesh in corners and control joints reduces the risk. Fine cracks are usually cosmetic and easy to patch, but wider cracks should be checked by a renderer.

deck-sanding-and-sealing.q: How much does deck sanding and sealing cost in Australia?
deck-sanding-and-sealing.a: Deck sanding and sealing typically costs $35 to $70 per square metre in Australia, including sanding, cleanup, and two coats of exterior decking oil (around $70 to $296 per 10 litre tin). A standard 20 to 30 square metre deck usually runs $700 to $2,100 depending on timber condition and access.

deck-sanding-and-sealing.q: How often should a timber deck be sanded and resealed?
deck-sanding-and-sealing.a: Most timber decks need resealing with oil or stain every one to two years to keep water resistance up, while a full sand back is usually only needed every five to ten years once the timber greys, splinters, or the old coating flakes badly. Sun exposure and foot traffic speed up wear.

deck-sanding-and-sealing.q: Can I sand and seal a deck myself?
deck-sanding-and-sealing.a: Sanding and sealing a deck yourself is a realistic DIY job with a hired drum or orbital sander, though it is physically demanding and dusty. Getting even coverage on oil and avoiding lap marks takes practice, so many homeowners hire a professional for decks over about 20 square metres.

fence-gate-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a fence gate in Australia?
fence-gate-installation.a: A single fence gate installation costs $150 to $400 in Australia, covering hinge and latch hardware ($17 to $85) plus timber framing and labour at standard fencing rates of $100 to $180 per metre. Wider double gates or steel driveway gates cost more due to extra bracing and hardware.

fence-gate-installation.q: What makes a gate sag over time?
fence-gate-installation.a: Gates sag mainly from undersized hinges, posts that were not set deep enough in concrete, or timber framing that lacks a diagonal brace. Heavier gates put more strain on the top hinge in particular. Fitting a diagonal turnbuckle brace and using galvanised hinges rated for the gate weight prevents most sagging.

fence-gate-installation.q: How long does it take to install a fence gate?
fence-gate-installation.a: A single fence gate installation usually takes half a day to a full day once posts are set, including trimming and fitting hardware. Concrete around new posts needs 24 to 48 hours to cure before the gate can safely take weight, so tradespeople often return the next day to hang it.

garden-path-paving.q: How much does garden path paving cost in Australia?
garden-path-paving.a: Garden path paving costs $50 to $150 per square metre installed in Australia, including concrete pavers (around $15 each for a 400x400mm size), bedding sand, and a compacted crusher dust base. A narrow one metre wide path across a typical backyard usually lands toward the lower end of that range.

garden-path-paving.q: What is the best base for a garden path?
garden-path-paving.a: A compacted crusher dust base over a layer of road base is the standard foundation for a garden path in Australia, giving pavers a stable, well drained surface that resists shifting. Skipping proper compaction is the most common cause of pavers sinking or going uneven within a year or two.

garden-path-paving.q: Can I lay a garden path myself?
garden-path-paving.a: Laying a simple garden path is a realistic DIY project for a straight, narrow path over firm ground, using pavers, sand, and a hand tamper. Curved paths, sloped sites, or areas near tree roots are harder to get level and drained properly, so those jobs are usually better left to a paver.

house-slab-pouring.q: How much does it cost to pour a house slab in Australia?
house-slab-pouring.a: Pouring a house slab costs $50 to $150 per square metre in Australia, including reinforcing mesh, formwork, and concrete. A standard 100 to 150 square metre home slab typically totals $5,000 to $22,500 depending on soil conditions, site access, and whether extra excavation or engineering is required.

house-slab-pouring.q: How thick does a house slab need to be?
house-slab-pouring.a: A standard residential house slab is usually poured around 100mm thick for the main area, with thickened edge beams and footings sized by an engineer based on soil classification. Reactive clay soils often need a thicker, more heavily reinforced slab than sand or rock, which is why engineering reports vary in cost.

house-slab-pouring.q: How long does a house slab need to cure before building?
house-slab-pouring.a: A house slab reaches enough strength to build on after about seven days, though full concrete strength takes around 28 days to develop. Builders typically wait at least a week before starting frame work, and formwork is usually stripped after two to three days once the edges have set.

leaf-guard-installation.q: How much does leaf guard installation cost in Australia?
leaf-guard-installation.a: Leaf guard installation costs $30 to $80 per metre in Australia, including gutter mesh (around $285 a roll) and fitting along the existing gutter line. A typical single storey home with 30 to 40 metres of guttering usually costs $900 to $3,200 depending on roof pitch and access.

leaf-guard-installation.q: Does leaf guard stop gutters blocking completely?
leaf-guard-installation.a: Leaf guard mesh significantly reduces blockages by keeping out leaves and larger debris, but it does not stop everything. Fine debris like gum leaves, pine needles, or seed pods can still build up on top of the mesh over time, so gutters still need an occasional clean, just far less often.

leaf-guard-installation.q: Can I install gutter leaf guard myself?
leaf-guard-installation.a: Installing gutter leaf guard yourself is possible for a single storey home with safe roof access, using clip-in or screw-fix mesh sold at hardware stores. Two storey homes or steep roofs are safer left to a professional, since most leaf guard injuries come from ladder falls rather than the job itself.

plasterboard-installation.q: Is plasterboard the same as Gyprock?
plasterboard-installation.a: Plasterboard is the generic term for gypsum board, while Gyprock is a specific brand of plasterboard made by CSR, similar to how Kleenex is a brand of tissue. Tradespeople in Australia often say Gyprock out of habit even when installing a different brand like Boral or USG, since the products are functionally the same.

9mm plasterboard suits ceilings on closely spaced trusses and standard wall linings in most homes, while 12mm plasterboard is the sturdier choice for walls needing extra strength or wider stud spacing. Wet areas and garage walls often use the thicker 12mm sheet for better impact resistance and fire performance.

plasterboard-installation.q: How much does plasterboard installation cost in Australia?
plasterboard-installation.a: Plasterboard installation costs $45 to $90 per hour for a plasterer in Australia, with sheets themselves running $28 to $97 each depending on size and thickness. A standard room typically needs several sheets plus base coat, jointing tape, and topping compound, adding roughly $80 to $150 in material costs on top of labour.

ridge-capping-repair.q: How much does ridge capping repair cost in Australia?
ridge-capping-repair.a: Ridge capping repair costs $50 to $100 an hour for a roofer in Australia, with most jobs taking two to four hours depending on how many ridge lengths need repointing or replacing. Materials add roughly $40 for flexible roof pointing plus around $50 per metre of new Colorbond capping if sections are damaged.

ridge-capping-repair.q: What causes ridge capping to fail?
ridge-capping-repair.a: Ridge capping usually fails when the old cement pointing that seals it to the tiles or sheets dries out, shrinks, and cracks over 15 to 20 years, letting water in underneath. Storm damage, tile movement, and corrosion on metal roofs can also loosen ridge capping earlier than that.

ridge-capping-repair.q: How do I know if my ridge capping needs repair?
ridge-capping-repair.a: Signs your ridge capping needs repair include visible cracks or gaps in the pointing along the roof ridge, ceiling stains after rain, capping that looks lifted or loose, and crumbling cement visible from the ground. A roofer can confirm the extent of the damage during an on-roof inspection before quoting.

skylight-installation.q: How much does skylight installation cost in Australia?
skylight-installation.a: Skylight installation costs $900 to $3,500 in Australia including the skylight unit and roofer's labour, depending on the type. Tubular skylights run from about $770 to $2,700 for the unit alone, plus flashing (around $65) and typically half a day of roofing labour at $50 to $100 an hour.

skylight-installation.q: What are the downsides of skylights?
skylight-installation.a: The main downsides of skylights are heat gain in summer, potential heat loss in winter without double glazing, and the risk of leaks if flashing is fitted poorly or ages without maintenance. Tubular skylights avoid most of these issues since they use a small roof-level dome rather than a large glass panel.

A well installed skylight with correctly fitted flashing should not leak, and most leaks trace back to deteriorated flashing seals, cracked sealant, or debris build up around the unit rather than the skylight itself. Getting flashing checked every few years, especially after storms, prevents most water ingress problems before they start.

tile-regrouting.q: How much does tile regrouting cost in Australia?
tile-regrouting.a: Tile regrouting costs $15 to $40 per square metre in Australia for labour, since the job is mostly removing old grout and repacking new grout rather than buying tiles. A standard bathroom typically costs $300 to $700 total, with grout itself only adding about $12 to $33 per 5kg bag.

tile-regrouting.q: How often should tile grout be redone?
tile-regrouting.a: Tile grout typically needs redoing every 10 to 15 years in normal areas, but wet areas like showers can need it sooner, often every 5 to 8 years, once grout turns porous, stains, or starts crumbling. Regrouting before grout fails completely helps prevent water getting behind tiles and causing hidden damage.

Regrouting tiles yourself is achievable for a small area with a grout removal tool, new grout, and a rubber float, and many homeowners tackle a splashback or small bathroom this way. Showers and large wet areas are trickier because poor grout removal or sealing can let water through, so mistakes cost more to fix.

wall-tiling.q: How much does wall tiling cost in Australia?
wall-tiling.a: Wall tiling costs $45 to $120 per square metre installed in Australia, including ceramic tiles (around $14 to $59 per square metre), adhesive, and grout. A standard bathroom or kitchen splashback wall typically costs $500 to $1,500 total depending on tile size, pattern complexity, and how much surface prep is needed first.

wall-tiling.q: Do I need to waterproof a wall before tiling?
wall-tiling.a: Wet areas like showers need a waterproofing membrane applied before tiling, while splashbacks and other dry walls generally do not. Skipping waterproofing in a shower risks water tracking through grout lines into the wall cavity, leading to mould and hidden damage that costs far more to fix later than the membrane itself would have.

wall-tiling.q: What size tiles make a small bathroom wall look bigger?
wall-tiling.a: Larger format tiles, generally 300x600mm or bigger, make a small bathroom wall look bigger by reducing the number of grout lines breaking up the surface. Lighter colours and a single tile run floor to ceiling add to the effect. Small mosaic tiles tend to visually shrink a space despite being popular for feature strips.

acrylic-rendering.q: How much does acrylic rendering cost in Australia?
acrylic-rendering.a: Acrylic rendering typically costs $30 to $80 per square metre installed, covering labour and materials. A 15-litre bucket of acrylic render runs close to $213, plus reinforcing mesh at $46 to $56 a roll for larger jobs. Final price depends on wall condition, the number of coats needed and whether old render must be stripped first.

acrylic-rendering.q: What is the difference between acrylic render and cement render?
acrylic-rendering.a: Acrylic render is a premixed, flexible coating with polymers added for crack resistance and colour consistency, while cement render is a sand-and-cement mix applied then painted separately. Acrylic dries faster and resists hairline cracking better on masonry veneer, though the premixed product itself costs more than a basic sand-and-cement mix.

acrylic-rendering.q: How long does acrylic render last?
acrylic-rendering.a: Acrylic render generally lasts 15 to 20 years before it needs recoating, longer than traditional cement render because its flexible polymer binder resists cracking. Lifespan depends on climate exposure, surface preparation and application quality. Regular washing and prompt repair of any cracks help acrylic render hold its finish and colour for the full period.

bathroom-tiling.q: How much does bathroom tiling cost in Australia?
bathroom-tiling.a: Bathroom tiling is usually quoted as part of a broader bathroom renovation, which runs $15,000 to $35,000 in Australia including tiles, waterproofing and fixtures. Porcelain floor tiles cost $28.90 to $125 per square metre and wall tiles $14 to $58.90 per square metre, plus adhesive and grout, before installation labour is added.

bathroom-tiling.q: Do you need to waterproof a bathroom before tiling?
bathroom-tiling.a: Yes. Wet areas like showers and floors need a waterproof membrane applied and cured before any tiles go down, because tiles and grout alone are not watertight. Skipping this step risks leaks into walls and subfloors down the track. A liquid membrane plus primer typically costs a few hundred dollars in materials for a small bathroom.

bathroom-tiling.q: Can you tile over existing bathroom tiles?
bathroom-tiling.a: Tiling over existing tiles is possible if the old tiles are sound, flat and well bonded, using a suitable primer and adhesive. It adds height to the floor and is not recommended in wet areas without fresh waterproofing underneath. Most tilers prefer removing old tiles first to check for hidden damage or mould.

colorbond-gutter-installation.q: How much does Colorbond guttering cost per metre in Australia?
colorbond-gutter-installation.a: Colorbond guttering typically costs $30 to $80 per metre installed in Australia, including labour and materials. A length of Colorbond quad gutter itself runs about $20 to $50 from suppliers, with Colorbond downpipes adding $7 to $37 per length. Final price depends on gutter profile, roof height and how much old guttering needs removing first.

colorbond-gutter-installation.q: Is Colorbond steel made in Australia?
colorbond-gutter-installation.a: Yes. Colorbond steel is manufactured in Australia by BlueScope at its Port Kembla plant in New South Wales, using a mix of local and imported steel. It has been produced locally since the 1960s and remains the standard prepainted steel used for Australian roofs, gutters, fencing and downpipes.

colorbond-gutter-installation.q: What is Colorbond gutter made of?
colorbond-gutter-installation.a: Colorbond gutter is roll-formed from zinc-and-aluminium-coated steel that is then given a baked-on colour coating for corrosion resistance and UV stability. This combination lets it handle harsh Australian weather without rusting or fading quickly, which is why it has largely replaced plain galvanised steel guttering on new homes.

deck-staining-and-painting.q: How much does it cost to stain and paint a deck in Australia?
deck-staining-and-painting.a: Deck staining and painting costs $40 to $70 per hour for a professional painter, with most standard-sized decks taking a day or two of labour once sanding and prep are included. A 10-litre tin of decking oil or stain costs $70 to $296 depending on the brand and finish, covering roughly 40 to 50 square metres per coat.

deck-staining-and-painting.q: How often should you restain a deck in Australia?
deck-staining-and-painting.a: Most Australian decks need restaining every one to two years, or sooner in coastal or high-sun areas where UV exposure fades and dries out the timber faster. Signs it is time include greying wood, peeling finish or water no longer beading on the surface. Regular recoating protects the timber and avoids costly sanding and repair later.

deck-staining-and-painting.q: Do you need to sand a deck before staining it?
deck-staining-and-painting.a: Yes, sanding removes the old, worn finish, greyed timber fibres and rough grain so the new stain can soak in evenly and bond properly. Skipping this step usually means patchy colour and a shorter-lasting finish. A light sand between coats on a well-maintained deck is often enough, while neglected decks need a full sand back.

fence-painting.q: How much does it cost to paint a fence in Australia?
fence-painting.a: Fence painting costs $40 to $70 per hour for a painter, with most standard timber fences taking a few hours to a full day depending on length and condition. A 10-litre tin of exterior acrylic paint costs $28.50 to $108.90 and typically covers 40 to 100 square metres per coat, so materials for an average fence run well under $200.

fence-painting.q: What paint is best for an outdoor timber fence?
fence-painting.a: Exterior acrylic paint is the standard choice for Australian timber fences because it flexes with the timber, resists UV fading and handles rain better than interior paint. A primer or undercoat is worth using on bare or weathered timber first. Oil-based options exist too, but acrylic is easier to maintain and recoat over time.

fence-painting.q: How often should a fence be repainted?
fence-painting.a: Most timber fences need repainting every three to five years, though fences facing full sun or coastal salt air can fade and crack sooner. Watch for peeling, chalking or bare patches as the cue to recoat rather than waiting a fixed number of years. Cleaning and priming worn sections first makes the new coat last longer.

gas-hot-water-system-repair.q: How much does gas hot water system repair cost in Australia?
gas-hot-water-system-repair.a: Gas hot water repairs are billed at $80 to $200 an hour for a licensed plumber, so a straightforward fix like a faulty thermocouple or pilot light often costs $150 to $400 in labour. If the unit itself needs replacing rather than repairing, a new gas instantaneous system costs $895 to $2,499 before installation.

gas-hot-water-system-repair.q: How long do gas hot water systems last?
gas-hot-water-system-repair.a: Gas hot water systems typically last 8 to 12 years for storage tanks and up to 15 to 20 years for continuous flow units with regular servicing. Age, water quality and how often the unit is used all affect lifespan. Once a storage tank starts leaking or rusting, repair is usually not worthwhile and replacement is the better option.

gas-hot-water-system-repair.q: Why does my gas hot water system keep going out?
gas-hot-water-system-repair.a: A gas hot water system that keeps cutting out is usually caused by a faulty thermocouple, blocked pilot light, gas supply issue or a failing thermostat. Dirty burners and poor ventilation can also trigger safety shutoffs. A licensed gas plumber needs to diagnose the exact cause, since gas appliances should not be opened up by homeowners.

hybrid-flooring-installation.q: How much does hybrid flooring installation cost in Australia?
hybrid-flooring-installation.a: Hybrid flooring installation costs $40 to $150 per square metre supplied and fitted in Australia. The flooring itself runs $31 to $99 per square metre depending on quality and thickness, with skirting boards adding a few dollars per linear metre. Final price depends on subfloor condition, room size and whether old flooring needs removing first.

hybrid-flooring-installation.q: What is hybrid flooring made of?
hybrid-flooring-installation.a: Hybrid flooring combines a rigid core, usually a mix of limestone composite and PVC, with a printed timber-look layer and a wear-resistant top coating. This construction makes it more water-resistant than laminate and more stable than vinyl planks, which is why it has become a popular choice for Australian kitchens, living areas and bathrooms.

Most hybrid flooring is highly water-resistant rather than fully waterproof, meaning spills and splashes are fine if wiped up reasonably quickly. Standing water left for extended periods can still seep into joints over time. It handles moisture far better than laminate or timber, which is why it suits bathrooms, laundries and kitchens so well.

leaking-shower-repair.q: How much does it cost to fix a leaking shower in Australia?
leaking-shower-repair.a: Fixing a leaking shower typically costs $30 to $80 per square metre for waterproofing and tiling work, billed through a licensed plumber or waterproofer at $80 to $200 an hour. A simple regrout and reseal with a leak repair kit and silicone can cost under $100 in materials, while a full waterproofing membrane replacement runs into the thousands.

leaking-shower-repair.q: What causes a shower to leak?
leaking-shower-repair.a: Shower leaks usually come from failed silicone seals, cracked or missing grout, a damaged waterproof membrane behind the tiles, or a faulty shower base or hob. Water finds its way through these gaps and can damage walls, floors and rooms below before it is noticed. Identifying the exact source usually needs a professional inspection rather than guesswork.

leaking-shower-repair.q: Can you repair a leaking shower without removing the tiles?
leaking-shower-repair.a: Minor leaks caused by failed silicone or grout can often be fixed by regrouting and resealing without removing tiles. But if the waterproof membrane underneath has failed, tiles usually need to come off so the membrane can be properly replaced. Patching over a membrane failure without removing tiles rarely stops the leak for good.

pool-paving.q: How much does pool paving cost in Australia?
pool-paving.a: Pool paving costs $50 to $150 per square metre installed for concrete or clay pavers in Australia. Natural stone runs higher: travertine pavers cost $109 to $359 per square metre supplied, so a stone pool surround commonly lands at $150 to $450 per square metre installed depending on groundwork.

pool-paving.q: What is the best paving for around a pool?
pool-paving.a: Travertine and other light-coloured natural stone pavers are popular around Australian pools because they stay cooler underfoot in summer than dark pavers or concrete. A non-slip or honed finish is important for safety on wet surfaces. Porcelain and textured concrete pavers are cheaper alternatives that still perform well if properly sealed and laid on a stable base.

pool-paving.q: Does pool paving need to be non-slip?
pool-paving.a: Yes, paving around a pool should have a slip-resistant surface since the area is constantly wet from swimmers and splashing. Honed, tumbled or textured finishes provide better grip than smooth, polished pavers. Most professional installers choose a slip rating suited to pool surrounds specifically, rather than general outdoor paving, to reduce the risk of falls.

roof-insulation-top-up.q: How much does roof insulation top-up cost in Australia?
roof-insulation-top-up.a: Topping up roof insulation costs $10 to $25 per square metre installed in Australia, depending on the current R-value and how much extra coverage is needed. A pack of R4.0 ceiling insulation batts costs $61 to $124 from Bunnings, so a DIY top-up on a small area can be far cheaper than a full professional insulation job.

roof-insulation-top-up.q: How do I know if my roof insulation needs topping up?
roof-insulation-top-up.a: Signs your roof insulation needs topping up include patchy or thin coverage visible from the manhole, rooms that feel hotter in summer or colder in winter than they should, and batts that are compressed, damp or gapped around downlights and edges. A quick inspection in the roof cavity usually shows whether existing insulation has settled or degraded.

roof-insulation-top-up.q: Can you add new insulation batts over old ones?
roof-insulation-top-up.a: Yes, adding a new layer of batts over existing insulation is a common way to boost the R-value without removing the old material, as long as it is still dry and in reasonable condition. Batts should be laid perpendicular to the layer below to cover gaps. Damaged, wet or compressed insulation should be replaced rather than covered over.

small-bathroom-renovation.q: How much does a small bathroom renovation cost in Australia?
small-bathroom-renovation.a: A small bathroom renovation typically costs $15,000 to $35,000 in Australia, covering the vanity, toilet, shower screen, waterproofing, tiling and an exhaust fan. Costs sit toward the lower end for cosmetic updates and higher when layout changes, new plumbing or structural work are involved. Trade quality, tile choice and fixture brand all shift the final figure.

small-bathroom-renovation.q: What is included in a small bathroom renovation?
small-bathroom-renovation.a: A typical small bathroom renovation includes a new vanity, toilet, shower screen, waterproofing membrane, wall and floor tiling, tapware and an exhaust fan. Many jobs also involve replacing plumbing rough-in and electrical wiring behind the walls. Because a small bathroom has less floor area, labour is often similar to a larger room even though material quantities are lower.

small-bathroom-renovation.q: Can a small bathroom be renovated without moving plumbing?
small-bathroom-renovation.a: Yes, keeping the toilet, shower and vanity in their existing positions is the cheapest way to renovate a small bathroom, since it avoids relocating drains and water lines. This like-for-like approach still allows for new tiles, fixtures and a fresh layout of finishes. Moving plumbing adds significant cost and is usually only worth it for a full layout change.

timber-floor-sanding-and-polishing.q: How much does timber floor sanding and polishing cost in Australia?
timber-floor-sanding-and-polishing.a: Timber floor sanding and polishing costs $40 to $150 per square metre in Australia, depending on the floor's condition and the number of coats applied. A 10-litre tin of polyurethane finish costs $60 to $318, with most floors needing two to three coats. Badly damaged or gappy floors sit near the top of that range due to extra prep work.

timber-floor-sanding-and-polishing.q: How often should timber floors be sanded and polished?
timber-floor-sanding-and-polishing.a: Timber floors generally need a full sand and polish every 7 to 10 years, though high-traffic homes or floors with a worn finish may need it sooner. A lighter recoat, without sanding back to bare timber, can often be done every few years to refresh the surface and extend the time between full sands.

timber-floor-sanding-and-polishing.q: How long does it take for polished timber floors to dry?
timber-floor-sanding-and-polishing.a: Polyurethane floor finishes are typically dry to walk on in socks within 24 hours per coat, but need 7 to 10 days to fully cure before rugs, furniture or heavy foot traffic return. Water-based finishes dry faster than oil-based ones. Rushing this stage risks scuffing or marking the new finish before it has properly hardened.

water-damage-plaster-repair.q: How much does water damage plaster repair cost in Australia?
water-damage-plaster-repair.a: Water damage plaster repair costs $45 to $90 an hour for a plasterer in Australia, with small ceiling or wall patches often done in a few hours once the leak causing the damage is fixed. A sheet of plasterboard costs $28 to $97, plus jointing compound and tape, so materials for a typical patch run well under $150.

water-damage-plaster-repair.q: Can you repair water-damaged plaster without replacing the whole sheet?
water-damage-plaster-repair.a: Yes, small water-stained or soft patches can often be cut out and patched with a new piece of plasterboard, jointing compound and tape rather than replacing the entire sheet. Badly sagging, crumbling or mould-affected plaster usually needs a larger section removed. Fixing the source of the leak first is essential, or the repair will fail again.

water-damage-plaster-repair.q: How do you know if water-damaged plaster needs replacing?
water-damage-plaster-repair.a: Plaster usually needs replacing rather than just patching when it is soft, sagging, crumbling to the touch, or showing mould growth, since the paper facing and gypsum core have broken down. Discolouration alone without softness can sometimes be painted over once dry. A plasterer can press-test the area to check whether the board has genuinely lost integrity.

ag-pipe-installation.q: How much does ag pipe installation cost in Australia?
ag-pipe-installation.a: Ag pipe drainage typically costs $300 to $2,000 per job in Australia, depending on trench length and site access. Materials are affordable, a 20 metre roll of slotted ag pipe costs $8 to $21 plus gravel backfill, but labour for digging, laying and connecting to a discharge point makes up most of the price.

ag-pipe-installation.q: What is ag pipe used for?
ag-pipe-installation.a: Ag pipe, short for agricultural pipe, is a slotted plastic pipe wrapped in a fabric sock, laid underground to collect and divert excess groundwater away from foundations, retaining walls and garden beds. It prevents waterlogging and rising damp by channelling water to a stormwater connection or soakwell before it pools against a structure.

ag-pipe-installation.q: How deep should ag pipe be installed?
ag-pipe-installation.a: Ag pipe is usually laid in a trench 300mm to 600mm deep, resting on a bed of gravel with the pipe's fabric sock facing up, and sloped gently toward the discharge point. Depth depends on what is being drained, footing drains sit deeper than garden bed drainage, and on local soil conditions.

bluestone-paving.q: How much does bluestone paving cost in Australia?
bluestone-paving.a: Bluestone paving costs $100 to $300 per square metre installed in Australia, covering both supply and labour. The bluestone pavers alone run $15 to $31 per square metre, with the remainder going to base preparation, sand bedding and skilled laying. Prices climb further for intricate patterns, honed finishes or difficult site access.

bluestone-paving.q: Why is bluestone paving so expensive?
bluestone-paving.a: Bluestone is expensive because it is dense basalt, quarried and precision-cut into pavers through a slow, labour-intensive process compared with manufactured concrete pavers. Its weight adds freight costs, and steady demand for its durable, non-fading grey tone keeps prices firm. Expect to pay $100 to $300 per square metre installed.

bluestone-paving.q: What is bluestone paving used for?
bluestone-paving.a: Bluestone paving is used for driveways, courtyards, pool surrounds and garden paths, because its dense basalt surface resists cracking, fading and heavy foot or vehicle traffic. It is especially popular on Victorian and Melbourne homes for its classic grey tone and non-slip texture when honed, sawn or tumbled for a natural finish.

coloured-concrete.q: How much does coloured concrete cost in Australia?
coloured-concrete.a: Coloured concrete costs $50 to $150 per square metre installed in Australia, typically $10 to $20 more than plain concrete because of oxide pigment and sealing. Oxide pigment costs $19 to $30 per pack, and a quality sealer to protect the colour runs $89 to $172 for a 4 litre tin.

Concrete is coloured by mixing oxide pigment powder into the wet mix before pouring, or by applying a dry-shake hardener across the surface for deeper, more even colour. Once cured, a sealer is applied to protect the pigment from UV fading, staining and efflorescence over time.

coloured-concrete.q: Does coloured concrete fade over time?
coloured-concrete.a: Coloured concrete can fade with UV exposure and heavy foot traffic, but a quality sealer slows this considerably and is usually reapplied every two to three years. Darker oxide colours tend to show fading and efflorescence more noticeably than lighter, natural tones, so regular resealing keeps the finish looking fresh.

downpipe-installation.q: What is the purpose of a downpipe?
downpipe-installation.a: A downpipe carries rainwater from your roof gutters down to the ground, a stormwater drain or a rainwater tank, stopping water pooling against your home's foundations and causing damp or erosion. Without working downpipes, gutters overflow during storms and water can pool dangerously close to walls and slabs.

downpipe-installation.q: What size downpipe do I need?
downpipe-installation.a: Most Australian homes use 90mm round or square Colorbond downpipes, though larger 100mm to 150mm downpipes suit bigger roof areas or high-rainfall regions. A licensed plumber calculates the right size from your roof's catchment area, ensuring gutters can drain fast enough during heavy storms without overflowing.

downpipe-installation.q: How much does downpipe installation cost in Australia?
downpipe-installation.a: Downpipe installation costs $30 to $80 per metre in Australia, including materials and labour. A single Colorbond downpipe length costs $7 to $37 depending on colour and profile, with plumbers charging more for extra bends, underground stormwater connections or difficult roof access.

flat-pack-kitchen-installation.q: How much does a flat-pack kitchen installation cost in Australia?
flat-pack-kitchen-installation.a: A full flat-pack kitchen renovation typically costs $20,000 to $45,000 installed in Australia, sitting toward the lower end of that range compared with custom joinery. Flat-pack base cabinets alone cost $69 to $306 each, with a laminate benchtop adding a further $110 to $135 per linear metre before labour.

flat-pack-kitchen-installation.q: Can I install a flat-pack kitchen myself?
flat-pack-kitchen-installation.a: Installing a flat-pack kitchen yourself is possible for confident DIYers, but getting cabinets level, plumb and securely fixed to wall studs takes real skill, and any plumbing or electrical work for the sink and appliances must be done by a licensed tradesperson. Most homeowners hire a carpenter for a straight, durable result.

flat-pack-kitchen-installation.q: How long does a flat-pack kitchen installation take?
flat-pack-kitchen-installation.a: A flat-pack kitchen installation usually takes two to five days for an average kitchen, depending on how many cabinets there are, whether benchtops need cutting to fit, and if plumbing or electrical connections are involved. Larger or L-shaped kitchens with an island bench can take noticeably longer.

glass-pool-fencing.q: How much does glass pool fencing cost in Australia?
glass-pool-fencing.a: Frameless glass pool fencing costs $400 to $800 per metre installed in Australia, with semi-frameless designs from around $250 per metre. The toughened panels alone cost $247 to $686 each, which is why glass costs more than aluminium or timber fencing. Compliance inspection fees can add to the total.

glass-pool-fencing.q: Does glass pool fencing need council approval in Australia?
glass-pool-fencing.a: Glass pool fencing must meet strict Australian pool safety requirements covering panel height, gaps and self-closing gates, and typically needs a compliance inspection before a pool can legally be used. Requirements vary by state and council, so check with your local authority or a licensed pool fencing installer before starting work.

glass-pool-fencing.q: What are the pros and cons of glass pool fencing?
glass-pool-fencing.a: Glass pool fencing gives an unobstructed view of the pool and a sleek, modern look, but it costs more than aluminium fencing, needs regular cleaning to stay streak-free, and toughened panels are heavier and pricier to replace if cracked. Frameless designs also need sturdy footings to stay rigid over time.

irrigation-solenoid-replacement.q: How much does it cost to replace an irrigation solenoid valve?
irrigation-solenoid-replacement.a: Replacing an irrigation solenoid valve sits toward the lower end of the $500 to $3,000 range irrigation contractors typically charge in Australia, since it is usually a single-valve swap rather than a full system job. The solenoid valve itself costs $30 to $64, with the rest covering the callout and labour.

irrigation-solenoid-replacement.q: What causes an irrigation solenoid valve to fail?
irrigation-solenoid-replacement.a: Irrigation solenoid valves typically fail from dirt or debris jamming the diaphragm, a burnt-out coil caused by an electrical fault, or general wear after years of cycling on and off. Signs include a zone that won't turn on or off, or a valve stuck open and flooding the lawn continuously.

irrigation-solenoid-replacement.q: Can I replace an irrigation solenoid myself?
irrigation-solenoid-replacement.a: Replacing an irrigation solenoid valve is a manageable DIY job for confident homeowners, since it usually just involves unscrewing the old solenoid and wiring in the new one. Correctly diagnosing whether the fault is the solenoid, the wiring or the controller is trickier, so many people still call an irrigation technician.

leaking-tap-repair.q: How much does it cost to fix a leaking tap in Australia?
leaking-tap-repair.a: Fixing a leaking tap costs $80 to $200 for a plumber's callout and hourly rate in Australia, with most simple washer or cartridge repairs finished within an hour. If the tap needs full replacement rather than a repair, a new mixer tap adds $93 to $326 on top of labour.

leaking-tap-repair.q: Why does my tap keep dripping after I replace the washer?
leaking-tap-repair.a: A tap that keeps dripping after a new washer usually has a worn or scored valve seat, a washer of the wrong size, or a failing cartridge in mixer-style taps. Mineral buildup and general age also stop a new washer sealing properly, so a plumber may need to resurface or replace the seat.

leaking-tap-repair.q: Can a leaking tap increase my water bill?
leaking-tap-repair.a: Yes, a leaking tap can waste a surprising amount of water over weeks and months, quietly pushing up your water bill even from what looks like a slow drip. Fixing it promptly is usually far cheaper than the wasted water, and a licensed plumber can typically resolve a dripping tap within an hour.

pop-up-sprinkler-installation.q: How much does pop-up sprinkler installation cost in Australia?
pop-up-sprinkler-installation.a: Pop-up sprinkler installation typically costs $500 to $3,000 in Australia, depending on how many sprinkler heads and zones your garden needs. Individual pop-up sprinkler heads cost $6 to $17 each, with poly pipe to connect them running $4 to $18 per 50 metre roll, before labour for trenching and connections.

Pop-up sprinklers sit flush with the lawn and rise on a spring-loaded stem once water pressure is applied, spraying a set pattern before retracting back below mower height when the zone finishes watering. They connect to buried poly pipe and are controlled by a timer or irrigation controller.

pop-up-sprinkler-installation.q: How many pop-up sprinklers do I need for my lawn?
pop-up-sprinkler-installation.a: The number of pop-up sprinklers you need depends on your lawn's size and shape, since each head typically covers a radius of three to five metres and spacing should let the spray patterns overlap. An irrigation installer maps your yard into zones based on water pressure and sprinkler spacing.

roof-leak-repair.q: How much does roof leak repair cost in Australia?
roof-leak-repair.a: Roof leak repair costs $50 to $100 per hour for a roofer in Australia, with most single-leak jobs like resealing flashing or replacing screws taking one to a few hours. Materials are cheap, roofing screws and silicone sealant together cost under $65, so labour and roof access make up most of the bill.

roof-leak-repair.q: What causes a roof to leak?
roof-leak-repair.a: Roof leaks are commonly caused by cracked or lifted flashing around chimneys and vents, rusted or popped roofing screws, damaged ridge capping, or blocked gutters overflowing back under the roofline. Storm damage and ageing sealant around penetrations are also frequent culprits, especially on older Colorbond and tiled roofs.

roof-leak-repair.q: Can I repair a roof leak myself?
roof-leak-repair.a: Minor roof leaks, like a loose screw or cracked sealant, can sometimes be patched temporarily by a confident DIYer, but working at height on a roof is dangerous and finding the true source of a leak often takes real experience. Most homeowners call a licensed roofer to properly diagnose and fix it.

smart-irrigation-controller-installation.q: How much does a smart irrigation controller installation cost in Australia?
smart-irrigation-controller-installation.a: Smart irrigation controller installation costs $500 to $3,000 installed in Australia, though a straightforward swap of an existing controller sits toward the lower end. The controller unit itself costs $115 to $259, with the rest covering wiring, Wi-Fi setup and programming zones to weather-based watering schedules.

smart-irrigation-controller-installation.q: What does a smart irrigation controller do?
smart-irrigation-controller-installation.a: A smart irrigation controller automatically adjusts your watering schedule using local weather data, soil moisture and seasonal conditions, so your garden gets watered only when it actually needs it. Most models connect to Wi-Fi and let you control and monitor zones from a smartphone app, helping cut water waste.

smart-irrigation-controller-installation.q: Can I install a smart irrigation controller myself?
smart-irrigation-controller-installation.a: Installing a smart irrigation controller yourself is possible if you are simply replacing an existing controller and reconnecting the same valve wiring, since most units are designed for easy DIY setup. Adding new zones or wiring a controller into a system you don't fully understand is better left to a professional.

toilet-repair-and-replacement.q: How much does it cost to replace a toilet in Australia?
toilet-repair-and-replacement.a: Replacing a toilet costs $80 to $200 per hour for a plumber's labour in Australia, plus the cost of the new toilet suite itself, which ranges from $315 to $1,490 depending on the style and brand. A straightforward like-for-like swap usually takes one to two hours of labour.

toilet-repair-and-replacement.q: How do I know if my toilet needs repair or full replacement?
toilet-repair-and-replacement.a: A toilet usually just needs repair, such as a new cistern valve, flush button or wax seal, if it is running constantly, flushing weakly or leaking at the base. Full replacement makes more sense if the bowl is cracked, the toilet is very old and inefficient, or repairs keep failing.

toilet-repair-and-replacement.q: How long does it take to replace a toilet?
toilet-repair-and-replacement.a: Replacing a toilet typically takes a licensed plumber one to two hours for a straightforward like-for-like swap, including removing the old suite, resealing the outlet and connecting the new one. It can take longer if the floor waste position needs adjusting or the toilet is being relocated entirely.

waterproofing-and-tiling.q: How much does waterproofing and tiling cost in Australia?
waterproofing-and-tiling.a: Waterproofing and tiling a wet area costs $60 to $180 per square metre installed in Australia, driven mostly by tile choice. A 15 litre tub of waterproofing membrane costs $59 to $262, and porcelain floor tiles run $29 to $125 per square metre before adhesive, grout and labour.

Waterproofing a bathroom or wet area yourself is technically possible, but it demands precise membrane coverage at joints, corners and floor-wall junctions, and any gaps risk leaks into the walls and floors below that are costly to fix once tiled over. Because mistakes are expensive and hard to spot, most homeowners hire a licensed waterproofer.

waterproofing-and-tiling.q: What is the best waterproofing method for a bathroom?
waterproofing-and-tiling.a: The best waterproofing method for a bathroom is a liquid membrane, rolled on over a primer to fully seal floors, walls and shower recesses before tiling begins. It bonds seamlessly around corners, pipes and drains without joins, unlike sheet membranes, making it the standard choice for most Australian wet area renovations today.

aluminium-slat-fencing.q: How much does aluminium slat fencing cost in Australia?
aluminium-slat-fencing.a: Aluminium slat fencing costs $250 to $600 per metre installed in Australia, covering panels, posts and concrete footings. Prefabricated panels alone run roughly $354 to $1,069 depending on height and slat spacing, so the installed price scales with panel grade. Powder-coated custom colours sit at the upper end.

aluminium-slat-fencing.q: What is the difference between aluminium slat fencing and Colorbond fencing?
aluminium-slat-fencing.a: Aluminium slat fencing uses horizontal or vertical slats with gaps for airflow and a modern look, while Colorbond fencing is solid steel sheeting for full privacy and wind resistance. Aluminium costs more per metre but never rusts, needs no repainting and suits pool surrounds and boundary screening where style matters as much as privacy.

aluminium-slat-fencing.q: Does aluminium slat fencing rust in coastal areas?
aluminium-slat-fencing.a: Quality aluminium slat fencing will not rust because aluminium forms a thin, stable oxide layer that protects it from corrosion, unlike steel which rusts when exposed to moisture. This makes it a strong choice for coastal Australian properties, though it pays to check for stainless steel fixings since cheaper fittings can still corrode.

boundary-fence-replacement.q: How much does it cost to replace a boundary fence in Australia?
boundary-fence-replacement.a: Replacing a boundary fence in Australia typically costs $100–$180 per metre supplied and installed, depending on fence height, timber grade and ground conditions. A standard timber paling fence uses palings priced around $1.68–$3.56 each plus posts and rails, so a 20 metre boundary commonly lands between $2,000 and $3,600.

boundary-fence-replacement.q: Do neighbours have to split the cost of a boundary fence in Australia?
boundary-fence-replacement.a: In most Australian states, neighbours share the cost of a standard dividing fence equally under local fencing legislation, since it serves both properties. If you want a taller, more expensive or decorative fence than the standard, you typically pay the difference yourself, and getting agreement in writing before work starts avoids disputes later.

boundary-fence-replacement.q: How long does a timber boundary fence last in Australia?
boundary-fence-replacement.a: A treated pine boundary fence typically lasts 15–20 years in Australian conditions before palings need replacing, though harsh sun, termites and coastal salt air can shorten that lifespan. Regular checks for rot at the base of posts and prompt repair of loose palings help a boundary fence reach its full service life.

composite-decking-installation.q: How much does composite decking cost to install in Australia?
composite-decking-installation.a: Composite decking typically costs $200–$1,000 per square metre supplied and installed in Australia, well above treated pine because the boards themselves run $14–$30 per linear metre. The wide range reflects board brand, substructure complexity and site access, so always get a fixed quote for your exact deck size and shape.

composite-decking-installation.q: Is composite decking better than timber decking in Australia?
composite-decking-installation.a: Composite decking costs more upfront than treated pine or merbau but needs no oiling, sanding or staining, resists splintering and holds its colour through harsh Australian sun. Timber decking is cheaper to install and has a warmer natural look, but demands yearly maintenance, so the better choice depends on your budget and appetite for upkeep.

composite-decking-installation.q: How long does composite decking last?
composite-decking-installation.a: Composite decking commonly carries manufacturer warranties of 10–25 years and can last several decades with minimal upkeep, since the boards are made from recycled wood fibre and plastic that resist rot, fading and insect damage far better than solid timber. Actual lifespan still depends on installation quality and sun exposure.

downpipe-repair.q: How much does downpipe repair cost in Australia?
downpipe-repair.a: Downpipe repair in Australia typically costs $30–$80 per metre of guttering trade labour, or a simple call-out to reseal a joint or replace a short section often falls in the $150–$300 range. A full downpipe replacement costs more, with Colorbond downpipe material alone priced around $7–$37 per length.

downpipe-repair.q: What size are downpipes in Australia?
downpipe-repair.a: Standard residential downpipes in Australia are usually 90mm round or square Colorbond profiles, matched to the size of the connected gutter and the roof catchment area it drains. Larger roofs or high-rainfall regions sometimes need 100mm downpipes, so a repairer will confirm the existing size before ordering a matching replacement length.

downpipe-repair.q: How do I know if my downpipe needs repair or replacement?
downpipe-repair.a: Signs a downpipe needs attention include water pooling at the base, visible rust or splits in the metal, joints pulling apart, or water overflowing at the top during rain. Minor leaks and loose brackets can usually be repaired, but heavily rusted or badly dented Colorbond downpipes are generally cheaper to replace than patch.

floating-floor-installation.q: How much does floating floor installation cost in Australia?
floating-floor-installation.a: Floating floor installation in Australia typically costs $40–$150 per square metre supplied and installed, depending on whether you choose laminate, hybrid or engineered timber. Laminate boards alone run about $19–$64 per square metre plus underlay at roughly $14 per square metre, so material choice drives most of the price difference.

floating-floor-installation.q: What does a floating floor mean?
floating-floor-installation.a: A floating floor is a flooring system that clicks or locks together and rests on an underlay rather than being nailed or glued to the subfloor beneath it. This lets the boards expand and contract slightly with temperature and humidity, which is why laminate, hybrid and engineered timber floors are usually installed this way in Australian homes.

floating-floor-installation.q: Can you install a floating floor over tiles?
floating-floor-installation.a: Yes, a floating floor can generally be installed directly over existing tiles as long as the surface is flat, clean and free of loose or cracked sections. A thin foam or acoustic underlay sits between the tiles and the new boards, which also helps deaden sound and even out minor unevenness in the original floor.
