gutter-guard-installation.q: How much does gutter guard installation cost in Australia?
gutter-guard-installation.a: Gutter guard installation typically costs $30–$80 per metre installed in Australia, which includes the guttering trade's labour plus a mesh product priced from around $181–$584 per roll. A standard single storey home usually needs several rolls, so total price depends heavily on roof perimeter and roof pitch.

gutter-guard-installation.q: Can I install gutter guard myself?
gutter-guard-installation.a: Gutter guard mesh can be a DIY job on a single storey home with good ladder access, since the product simply clips or screws onto the existing gutter edge. Working at height on a two storey roof is riskier, though, and most Australian homeowners hire a guttering trade for safety and a neater, better sealed finish.

gutter-guard-installation.q: Is gutter guard worth it in Australia?
gutter-guard-installation.a: Gutter guard is generally worth it in Australia because it keeps leaves and debris out of the gutter, cutting the risk of blockages, overflow and ember attack during bushfire season. It also reduces how often you need to climb up and clean gutters manually, which for many homeowners offsets the upfront material and installation cost over time.

irrigation-system-installation.q: How much does it cost to install an irrigation system in Australia?
irrigation-system-installation.a: A residential irrigation system in Australia typically costs $500–$3,000 installed, depending on garden size, the number of zones and whether you choose drip line or pop-up sprinklers. A basic controller adds around $115–$259, while solenoid valves for each zone run roughly $30–$64 each on top of pipe and labour.

irrigation-system-installation.q: What is the best irrigation for watering grass?
irrigation-system-installation.a: Pop-up sprinklers on a timed controller are generally the best irrigation option for watering lawn areas, since they cover a wide radius evenly and retract flush with the grass when not running. Drip irrigation suits garden beds and shrubs better, as it targets roots directly and wastes far less water than overhead spray.

irrigation-system-installation.q: How long does it take to install an irrigation system?
irrigation-system-installation.a: A basic irrigation system for an average suburban garden usually takes 1–2 days to install, covering trenching for poly pipe, fitting sprinkler or drip zones, wiring the controller and testing each zone. Larger properties with multiple zones or more complex garden beds can take three days or more to complete properly.

lighting-installation.q: How much does it cost to install lighting in Australia?
lighting-installation.a: Lighting installation in Australia typically costs $70–$130 an hour for a licensed electrician, and most downlight jobs take 20–40 minutes per fitting once wiring is in place. LED downlights themselves cost around $13–$46 each, so installing six downlights commonly totals $300–$600 including labour and fittings.

lighting-installation.q: Do I need an electrician to install downlights in Australia?
lighting-installation.a: Yes, all fixed electrical lighting work in Australia must be carried out by a licensed electrician, since it involves connecting new fittings to mains wiring behind walls and ceilings. This is a legal requirement in every state and territory, and using an unlicensed installer can also create problems with home insurance and building compliance down the track.

lighting-installation.q: How many downlights do I need for a room?
lighting-installation.a: As a rough guide, allow one LED downlight for every 1.5–2 square metres of ceiling space for even general lighting, then adjust for task areas like kitchen benches or reading nooks. A qualified electrician can calculate exact spacing and wattage for your room size, ceiling height and how bright you want it.

power-point-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a power point in Australia?
power-point-installation.a: Installing a new power point in Australia typically costs $70–$130 an hour for a licensed electrician, with a straightforward job usually taking half an hour to an hour once cabling access is easy. A double GPO unit itself costs around $14–$62, so most single power point jobs land between $100 and $250 total.

power-point-installation.q: Can I install a power point myself in Australia?
power-point-installation.a: No, installing or wiring a power point yourself is illegal in Australia unless you hold an electrical licence, because it involves working on live mains circuits inside walls. All states require a licensed electrician to carry out fixed wiring work, and DIY electrical jobs can void home insurance and create a genuine fire or shock risk.

power-point-installation.q: How many power points can be added to a circuit?
power-point-installation.a: The number of new GPOs a circuit can safely take depends on the circuit's rating and what else is already connected, not a fixed number, so an electrician checks total load before adding outlets. Adding two or three double power points to an existing circuit is common, but heavier appliances may need their own dedicated circuit.

roof-painting.q: How much does roof painting cost in Australia?
roof-painting.a: Roof painting in Australia typically costs $40–$70 an hour for a professional painter, with most residential roofs taking a full crew several days once cleaning, priming and two coats are included. A 15 litre pail of roof membrane paint costs around $249, and an average roof needs several pails depending on size and pitch.

roof-painting.q: How often should a roof be repainted?
roof-painting.a: Most Australian roofs need repainting every 7–15 years, depending on the roofing material, paint quality and how much sun and weather the roof copes with. Tile roofs generally hold a coating longer than metal, and coastal or high-UV areas tend to need fresher coats sooner as the membrane breaks down faster in harsh conditions.

A roof paint or membrane coating can seal minor surface cracks and improve water shedding, but it is not a fix for structural leaks caused by broken tiles, failed flashing or rusted-through metal sheeting. Those problems need proper roof repair first, since painting over an active leak only hides the damage while water keeps getting in underneath.

smoke-alarm-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a smoke alarm in Australia?
smoke-alarm-installation.a: Smoke alarm installation in Australia typically costs $70–$130 an hour for a licensed electrician, with a straightforward single alarm swap often taking under an hour. A 240V photoelectric smoke alarm unit itself costs around $19–$75, so a single replacement commonly totals $100–$200 including labour and the alarm.

smoke-alarm-installation.q: How many smoke alarms does a house need in Australia?
smoke-alarm-installation.a: Smoke alarm requirements vary by state, but as a general rule most Australian homes need at least one alarm in every bedroom, one in hallways connecting bedrooms to the rest of the house, and one on every level. Photoelectric alarms are the type generally recommended, and checking your specific state's current rules is worthwhile before installing.

smoke-alarm-installation.q: What is the difference between a battery smoke alarm and a hardwired one?
smoke-alarm-installation.a: A battery smoke alarm runs on its own power source and is simpler to install, but needs regular battery checks and eventual replacement. A hardwired 240V smoke alarm connects to household mains power, usually with a battery backup, and can be interlinked with other alarms in the house so every unit sounds together when smoke is detected anywhere.

treated-pine-decking-installation.q: How much does treated pine decking cost to install in Australia?
treated-pine-decking-installation.a: Treated pine decking typically costs $200–$1,000 per square metre supplied and installed in Australia, sitting at the cheaper end of that decking range compared with composite or hardwood. The decking boards themselves cost roughly $4 per linear metre, with framing timber and decking screws adding to the total material cost.

treated-pine-decking-installation.q: How long does treated pine decking last?
treated-pine-decking-installation.a: Treated pine decking typically lasts 15–25 years when properly maintained with regular oiling or staining, since the H3 or H4 treatment protects the timber against rot and termites. Without upkeep it weathers faster, greying and splitting sooner, so ongoing maintenance matters more for treated pine than it does for composite decking.

treated-pine-decking-installation.q: Do you need to oil treated pine decking?
treated-pine-decking-installation.a: Yes, treated pine decking should be oiled or stained regularly, generally once a year in harsh sun and every 1–2 years in milder climates, to stop the timber from greying, cracking and drying out. The treatment itself protects against rot and termites, but oiling protects the surface and keeps the timber looking good.

waterproofing-membrane-installation.q: How much does waterproofing membrane installation cost in Australia?
waterproofing-membrane-installation.a: Waterproofing membrane installation typically costs $30–$80 per square metre in Australia, covering surface preparation, primer, the membrane itself and reinforcing at joints and corners. A 15 litre pail of liquid membrane costs around $59–$262, so a small bathroom or balcony job commonly totals a few hundred dollars in materials alone.

waterproofing-membrane-installation.q: Can I do waterproofing myself in Australia?
waterproofing-membrane-installation.a: Queensland requires wet-area waterproofing to be carried out by a licensed contractor, and every state requires it to meet the Australian wet-area waterproofing standard. DIY membrane products exist for minor repairs, but professional certification matters for insurance and resale, so check your state licensing rules before starting.

waterproofing-membrane-installation.q: What type of waterproofing membrane is best?
waterproofing-membrane-installation.a: Liquid-applied membranes are the most common choice for Australian bathrooms and balconies because they cure into a seamless, flexible coating that handles the tricky corners and pipe penetrations in a wet area well. Sheet membranes suit large flat areas like roof decks, so the best type really depends on the shape and use of the space being waterproofed.

artificial-turf-installation.q: How much does artificial turf installation cost in Australia?
artificial-turf-installation.a: Artificial turf installation in Australia typically costs $50–$150 per square metre installed, covering turf, crusher dust base, weed matting and labour. Synthetic turf material alone runs $13–$23 per square metre before installation costs are added. Prices rise for sloped yards, poor drainage or premium turf pile.

A proper artificial turf base starts with compacted crusher dust for drainage and stability, topped with a weed matting layer to stop growth pushing through. The turf is then laid, joined and pinned down, with sand or rubber infill brushed in for support. Skipping the base causes uneven, boggy lawns.

artificial-turf-installation.q: Is artificial turf worth it for an Australian backyard?
artificial-turf-installation.a: Artificial turf suits low-rainfall regions, shaded yards where grass struggles, and busy households wanting a low-maintenance lawn without mowing or watering. It costs more upfront than natural turf but avoids ongoing water and mowing costs. It heats up in direct summer sun and needs occasional brushing to keep the pile upright.

brick-paving-installation.q: How much does brick paving cost in Australia?
brick-paving-installation.a: Brick paving in Australia typically costs $50–$150 per square metre installed, covering clay brick pavers, sand and crusher dust base plus labour. Clay pavers themselves cost roughly $34–$50 each. Patterned laying, cutting around edges and site access can push costs toward the higher end of that range.

brick-paving-installation.q: What is the best base for brick paving?
brick-paving-installation.a: A solid brick paving base starts with compacted crusher dust or road base for drainage and stability, followed by a bedding layer of paving sand around 20–30mm deep. Bricks are laid on top, tapped level and jointed with sand. Skipping compaction is the main cause of sunken or wobbly pavers.

brick-paving-installation.q: Can I lay brick pavers myself?
brick-paving-installation.a: Laying brick pavers is a realistic DIY project for a flat, small area like a garden path, provided the base is properly excavated and compacted. Larger driveways or areas needing correct falls for drainage are best left to a professional paver, since poor compaction leads to costly resets. Tools can be hired.

concrete-path-installation.q: How much does a concrete path cost in Australia?
concrete-path-installation.a: A concrete path in Australia typically costs $50–$150 per square metre installed, covering formwork, reinforcing mesh, concrete mix and labour. A basic 20kg bag of concrete mix costs $9–$37 for small patch jobs, but paths are usually poured from bulk mixed truck concrete for consistency and strength.

concrete-path-installation.q: Is concrete the same as cement?
concrete-path-installation.a: Concrete and cement are not the same thing. Cement is a fine powder binder, usually Portland cement, that is mixed with water, sand and aggregate to make concrete. Concrete is the finished, hardened material used for paths, slabs and driveways. Cement alone is never used to pour a path.

concrete-path-installation.q: How much will 20kg of concrete cover?
concrete-path-installation.a: A 20kg bag of pre-mixed concrete covers roughly 0.01 cubic metres once mixed, enough for a small patch or post hole rather than a full path. For a standard 100mm thick concrete path, expect to need about one 20kg bag per 0.1 square metre, so bulk or truck-mixed concrete suits larger jobs.

drip-irrigation-installation.q: How much does drip irrigation installation cost in Australia?
drip-irrigation-installation.a: Drip irrigation installation in Australia typically costs $500–$3,000 fully installed, depending on garden size and zone complexity. A 30 metre roll of drip line costs $14–$31, while a basic irrigation controller adds $115–$259. Larger properties with multiple zones and automated controllers sit toward the top end.

drip-irrigation-installation.q: What is drip irrigation and how does it work?
drip-irrigation-installation.a: Drip irrigation delivers water slowly through small emitters along a poly pipe network, soaking the root zone directly rather than spraying leaves and paths. This cuts water waste from evaporation and runoff, suits garden beds and pots, and is usually run through a controller on a timed schedule for consistent watering.

drip-irrigation-installation.q: Can I install drip irrigation myself?
drip-irrigation-installation.a: Drip irrigation is one of the more DIY-friendly irrigation jobs, since kits connect to an existing tap with simple push-fit fittings and poly pipe. It suits small to medium gardens well. Larger properties needing multiple zones, buried mainlines or a smart controller tied into the water supply are better handled by a licensed installer.

floor-levelling.q: How much does floor levelling cost in Australia?
floor-levelling.a: Floor levelling in Australia typically costs $40–$150 per square metre, depending on how uneven the subfloor is and the flooring going on top. A 20kg bag of self-levelling compound costs $32–$70. Larger dips, timber subfloor repairs or full-room pours sit toward the higher end of that range.

floor-levelling.q: What is floor levelling compound made of?
floor-levelling.a: Self-levelling compound is a cement-based powder mixed with water into a pourable slurry that spreads and settles flat under its own weight. It bonds to concrete or timber subfloors and cures hard within hours, creating a smooth, even surface ready for tiles, vinyl, carpet or timber flooring to be laid over.

floor-levelling.q: Do I need floor levelling before laying tiles?
floor-levelling.a: Floor levelling is recommended before tiling whenever the subfloor has dips, humps or slopes greater than a few millimetres, since uneven substrates cause tiles to crack, lift or sit unevenly at joins. Timber, vinyl and floating floors are also sensitive to unevenness, so a level check before flooring work saves problems later.

gutter-replacement.q: How much do gutters cost in Australia?
gutter-replacement.a: Gutter replacement in Australia typically costs $30–$80 per metre installed, covering Colorbond guttering, downpipes and labour. Colorbond quad gutter runs $20–$50 per length, while a Colorbond downpipe adds $7–$37 per length. Total cost depends on roof size, gutter profile and how many downpipes are needed.

Installing gutters yourself is possible for a small shed or single straight run, but replacing house guttering usually means working at height, getting falls correct for drainage and matching flashing to the roofline. Incorrect falls cause pooling and overflow, so most homeowners use a licensed gutter installer for the full job.

gutter-replacement.q: What are signs gutters need replacing?
gutter-replacement.a: Common signs gutters need replacing include visible rust or corrosion, cracks, sagging sections pulling away from the fascia, and water overflowing during rain instead of draining through the downpipes. Peeling paint or water stains on the fascia board below the gutter line are also strong signs of a failing gutter system.

kitchen-benchtop-replacement.q: How much does it cost to replace a kitchen benchtop in Australia?
kitchen-benchtop-replacement.a: Replacing a kitchen benchtop in Australia typically costs $2,000–$15,000 depending on material and benchtop length. Laminate benchtop material alone runs $110–$135 per linear metre, making it one of the more budget-friendly upgrades. Stone benchtops sit well above this range, so material choice is the biggest cost driver.

kitchen-benchtop-replacement.q: What is the cheapest benchtop material for a kitchen?
kitchen-benchtop-replacement.a: Laminate is generally the cheapest kitchen benchtop material in Australia, costing around $110–$135 per linear metre supplied, well below stone or timber options. It is durable enough for everyday use and comes in a wide range of finishes, though it is more prone to heat and scratch damage than stone benchtops.

kitchen-benchtop-replacement.q: Can I replace a kitchen benchtop without replacing the cabinets?
kitchen-benchtop-replacement.a: Yes, replacing just the benchtop while keeping existing cabinets is common and cuts costs significantly compared to a full kitchen renovation. The old benchtop is removed, cabinet tops are checked for level, and the new benchtop is fixed down with construction adhesive. Sink and tap cutouts need to align with existing plumbing.

metal-roof-replacement.q: How much does a metal roof replacement cost in Australia?
metal-roof-replacement.a: Metal roof replacement in Australia typically costs $50–$100 per hour of labour, with Colorbond roof sheeting priced at $15–$22 per linear metre supplied. A full re-roof also needs sarking, screws, ridge capping and flashing, so total project cost depends heavily on roof size, pitch and access difficulty.

metal-roof-replacement.q: How long does a metal roof replacement take?
metal-roof-replacement.a: A typical metal roof replacement takes a few days to around a week for an average house, covering removal of old sheeting, fitting new sarking, laying Colorbond sheets and finishing with ridge capping and flashing. Larger or steeper roofs, bad weather, and structural repairs underneath can extend the timeframe considerably.

metal-roof-replacement.q: When should I replace my metal roof instead of repairing it?
metal-roof-replacement.a: A metal roof usually needs full replacement rather than repair once rust, corrosion or leaks are widespread across multiple sheets rather than isolated to one area. Fastener failure, sagging sheets, or a roof nearing the end of its coating life are also signs replacement is more cost-effective than ongoing patch repairs.

rainwater-tank-installation.q: Is it legal to collect rainwater in Australia?
rainwater-tank-installation.a: Yes, collecting rainwater is legal across Australia, and many councils allow tanks to supplement mains water for gardens, toilets and laundry use. Some states and councils set specific rules around tank overflow, backflow prevention and plumbing connections, so it is worth checking local council requirements before installing a rainwater tank.

rainwater-tank-installation.q: Can I drink rainwater collected in a tank?
rainwater-tank-installation.a: Rainwater collected in a well-maintained tank can be safe to drink in many parts of Australia, particularly in rural areas without mains water, provided the roof, gutters and tank are kept clean and a first-flush diverter is fitted. Filtration and regular tank maintenance are recommended, and town water is generally preferred where available.

rainwater-tank-installation.q: How much does a rainwater tank installation cost in Australia?
rainwater-tank-installation.a: Rainwater tank installation in Australia typically costs $80–$200 per hour of plumbing labour, on top of the tank itself. A slimline rainwater tank costs $788–$3,602 depending on capacity, plus stormwater pipe for overflow connections. Total cost depends on tank size, pump requirements and how far it sits from the house.

roof-rebedding-and-repointing.q: How much does roof rebedding and repointing cost in Australia?
roof-rebedding-and-repointing.a: Roof rebedding and repointing in Australia typically costs $50–$100 per hour of roofing labour, varying with roof size, pitch and how many ridge capping tiles need work. Flexible roof pointing compound costs around $40 per 10 litres, while cement for traditional bedding runs $9–$57 per 20kg bag.

roof-rebedding-and-repointing.q: What is the difference between roof rebedding and repointing?
roof-rebedding-and-repointing.a: Rebedding replaces the cement mortar bed that holds ridge capping tiles in place, while repointing applies a flexible coating over the top to seal and weatherproof it. Older tile roofs often need both done together, since cracked or crumbling bedding lets water in and repointing alone will not fix a failing base.

roof-rebedding-and-repointing.q: How often does a tile roof need rebedding and repointing?
roof-rebedding-and-repointing.a: Tile roof ridge capping needs rebedding and repointing once the mortar bed starts to crumble, crack or come loose, which happens gradually as the roof ages and the bedding dries out. Signs it is overdue include loose or wobbly ridge tiles, crumbling mortar visible from the ground, and water stains near the ridge line.

sprinkler-system-installation.q: How much does a sprinkler system cost to install in Australia?
sprinkler-system-installation.a: A sprinkler system installation in Australia typically costs $500–$3,000 fully installed, depending on lawn size and the number of zones. Pop-up sprinkler heads cost $6–$17 each, while a controller adds $115–$259. Larger yards needing more heads, trenching and a smart controller sit toward the higher end.

sprinkler-system-installation.q: What is the best type of sprinkler for a lawn?
sprinkler-system-installation.a: Pop-up sprinklers are generally the best option for lawns, since the heads retract flush with the grass when not in use and pop up only when watering, avoiding tripping hazards and mower damage. They connect to poly pipe and a solenoid valve, allowing each zone to be watered on its own schedule.

sprinkler-system-installation.q: Can I install a sprinkler system myself?
sprinkler-system-installation.a: A basic sprinkler system with a few pop-up heads on one zone is achievable for a confident DIYer, using poly pipe and push-fit fittings. Multi-zone systems needing a solenoid valve, buried mainline trenching and a controller wired correctly are more involved, and most homeowners hire a licensed irrigation installer for the full job.

underfloor-insulation.q: How much does underfloor insulation cost in Australia?
underfloor-insulation.a: Underfloor insulation in Australia typically costs $10–$25 per square metre installed, covering insulation panels and labour to fit them between floor joists. A pack of underfloor insulation panels costs $54–$106 at retail. Larger homes with more subfloor area or difficult crawl space access sit toward the higher end.

underfloor-insulation.q: What is the best underfloor insulation for an Australian home?
underfloor-insulation.a: Rigid foam or polyester underfloor insulation panels fitted snugly between floor joists are a common, effective choice for Australian homes, since they resist moisture better than batts in damp subfloor spaces. The right R-value depends on climate zone, so checking local building requirements before buying panels helps avoid under-insulating a floor.

underfloor-insulation.q: Is underfloor insulation worth it in Australia?
underfloor-insulation.a: Underfloor insulation is worth it for homes with a suspended timber floor over an open subfloor, since uninsulated floors let significant heat escape in winter and let heat in during summer. It improves year-round comfort and can reduce heating and cooling running costs, making it one of the more cost-effective insulation upgrades.

backyard-landscaping.q: How much does backyard landscaping cost in Australia?
backyard-landscaping.a: Backyard landscaping in Australia typically costs $50 to $150 per square metre, depending on turf, garden beds, and hardscaping involved. A modest backyard makeover might use Sir Walter buffalo turf at around $18 per square metre, garden soil, and mulch, while retaining walls and paving push jobs toward the top of that range. Get a few quotes to compare scope.

backyard-landscaping.q: How long does backyard landscaping take?
backyard-landscaping.a: Most backyard landscaping projects take one to two weeks from clearing to planting, though larger jobs with retaining walls, irrigation, or extensive paving can stretch to four weeks or more. Weather, soil conditions, and how much of the yard needs regrading all affect the timeline, so ask your landscaper for a realistic schedule before work starts.

backyard-landscaping.q: What's included in a backyard landscaping quote?
backyard-landscaping.a: A typical backyard landscaping quote covers site preparation, turf or garden bed installation, soil and mulch, and any retaining walls or edging in the design. Materials like turf run about $18 per square metre and mulch around $15 per 60-litre bag, with labour making up the rest. Always ask for a written, itemised quote before work begins.

burst-pipe-repair.q: How much does burst pipe repair cost in Australia?
burst-pipe-repair.a: Burst pipe repair in Australia typically costs $80 to $200 per hour, with most straightforward jobs taking one to two hours once the plumber has isolated the water. Replacement pipe adds $6 to $23 per 5-metre length for PEX or around $10 to $16 per metre for copper. Emergency after-hours callouts usually cost more.

burst-pipe-repair.q: Is a burst pipe covered by home insurance?
burst-pipe-repair.a: Most Australian home insurance policies cover sudden, accidental burst pipe damage such as water damage to floors or walls, though the repair of the pipe itself is sometimes excluded. Gradual leaks or wear-related failures are often not covered. Check your policy's product disclosure statement and contact your insurer promptly after a burst pipe.

burst-pipe-repair.q: How quickly should a burst pipe be repaired?
burst-pipe-repair.a: A burst pipe needs urgent attention, ideally within hours, because even a small leak can release a large volume of water quickly and cause serious damage. Shut off the mains water supply immediately, then call an emergency plumber. Acting fast limits damage to floors, walls, and belongings and keeps the eventual repair bill smaller.

concrete-paver-installation.q: How much does concrete paver installation cost in Australia?
concrete-paver-installation.a: Concrete paver installation in Australia typically costs $50 to $150 per square metre, including base preparation, sand bedding, and laying. Bedding sand and crusher dust each add roughly $10 to $21 per bag on top of the paver cost. Patterned laying, cutting around edges, and difficult site access can push a job toward the higher end of that range.

concrete-paver-installation.q: How long do concrete pavers last?
concrete-paver-installation.a: Well-installed concrete pavers typically last 25 to 50 years with basic maintenance such as resealing every few years and keeping joints topped up with sand. Lifespan depends on the base preparation, paver quality, and how much foot or vehicle traffic the area gets. Cracking is usually a sign of poor base compaction rather than the pavers themselves.

concrete-paver-installation.q: Can concrete pavers be laid over an existing concrete slab?
concrete-paver-installation.a: Concrete pavers can often be laid directly over an existing slab if it is sound, level, and draining properly, using a thin mortar bed or paver adhesive instead of a full sand base. Cracked, uneven, or poorly drained slabs usually need repair first. A paving contractor can check the slab's condition before quoting the job.

driveway-paving.q: How much does driveway paving cost in Australia?
driveway-paving.a: Driveway paving in Australia typically costs $50 to $150 per square metre, covering excavation, base preparation, and paver laying. Pavers themselves add roughly $11 per bag of crusher dust and $11 to $21 per bag of bedding sand on top of paver supply. A standard double driveway usually needs 40 to 60 square metres of paving.

driveway-paving.q: How long does driveway paving take?
driveway-paving.a: Most residential driveway paving jobs take two to five days, depending on the driveway's size, whether old concrete needs removing, and how much excavation and base work is required. Weather and access for machinery also affect the schedule. A paver should give a clear day-by-day timeline as part of the quote.

driveway-paving.q: What is the best material for a driveway in Australia?
driveway-paving.a: Concrete pavers, brick pavers, and poured concrete are the most common Australian driveway materials, each with different upkeep and looks. Pavers are easy to repair individually and resist cracking from ground movement, while poured concrete gives a seamless surface but shows cracks over time. Climate, soil type, and budget usually decide the best fit.

floor-tiling.q: How much does floor tiling cost in Australia?
floor-tiling.a: Floor tiling in Australia typically costs $45 to $120 per square metre installed, covering tile adhesive, grout, and labour. Porcelain floor tiles themselves typically run from about $29 to $85 per square metre before installation, so tile choice makes a big difference to the total. Levelling an uneven subfloor first adds further cost.

floor-tiling.q: How long does floor tiling take to dry?
floor-tiling.a: Tile adhesive typically needs 24 to 48 hours to cure enough to walk on, though full grouting usually waits at least 24 hours after tiling. The whole floor should be left to cure fully, often around seven days, before it takes heavy furniture or appliances. Humidity and tile size can extend these times.

floor-tiling.q: Can you tile over an existing floor?
floor-tiling.a: Tiling over an existing floor is often possible if the surface is flat, stable, and well bonded, using the right primer or adhesive for the substrate. Cracked tiles, timber floors that flex, or floors with loose sections usually need preparation or removal first. A tiler can assess the existing floor before quoting.

gyprock-repair.q: How much does gyprock repair cost in Australia?
gyprock-repair.a: Gyprock repair in Australia typically costs $45 to $90 per hour, and a small hole or crack usually takes one to three hours to patch, sand, and paint-ready finish, for a total around $100 to $300. Full sheet replacement costs more once a new $28 to $97 plasterboard sheet, jointing compound, and tape are added to the labour.

gyprock-repair.q: Is Gyprock the same as plasterboard?
gyprock-repair.a: Gyprock is a well-known brand name for plasterboard in Australia, and the two terms are often used interchangeably. Other manufacturers make their own plasterboard products under different brand names, but they perform the same job of lining internal walls and ceilings with a gypsum core between paper facings. All are repaired the same way.

Modern Gyprock plasterboard, made from gypsum and paper, contains no asbestos. Older homes can still have asbestos-containing wall sheeting that looks similar from the surface, so if you are unsure about a wall in an older property, have a sample tested before cutting, sanding, or drilling into it. A licensed tradesperson can arrange testing.

kitchen-sink-installation.q: How much does kitchen sink installation cost in Australia?
kitchen-sink-installation.a: Installing a kitchen sink in Australia typically costs $250 to $600 in labour for a straightforward swap using the existing plumbing, or $600 to $1,600 supply-and-installed for a new sink and mixer tap. Sinks retail from about $170 to $770 and mixer taps from $79 to $477, so fixture choice drives most of the total.

kitchen-sink-installation.q: Can I install a kitchen sink myself?
kitchen-sink-installation.a: Installing a kitchen sink yourself is possible for a straight swap if the new sink matches the existing cutout and plumbing connections. Anything involving new pipework, moving connections, or gas and water compliance is safer left to a licensed plumber, and getting it professionally installed also protects your home insurance and any product warranty.

kitchen-sink-installation.q: What size kitchen sink do I need?
kitchen-sink-installation.a: Kitchen sink sizing depends on your cabinet width and how you use the kitchen, with a single bowl suiting compact kitchens and a double bowl, priced from around $170 to $770, giving more room for washing and prep. Standard base cabinets are usually 600mm or 900mm wide, which limits the sink dimensions that will fit.

mosaic-tiling.q: How much does mosaic tiling cost in Australia?
mosaic-tiling.a: Mosaic tiling in Australia typically costs $45 to $120 per square metre installed, reflecting the extra time needed to lay small tiles precisely. Mosaic sheets themselves cost around $9 to $26 each, with tile adhesive and grout adding a further $27 to $94 combined. Intricate feature areas like splashbacks usually sit toward the top of the range.

mosaic-tiling.q: Where is mosaic tiling used in the home?
mosaic-tiling.a: Mosaic tiling is most popular for kitchen splashbacks, bathroom feature walls, and shower niches, where its small format handles curves and detail better than large tiles. It also works well on pool surrounds and outdoor feature strips because the extra grout lines add slip resistance. Many homeowners use it to highlight a single accent area.

mosaic-tiling.q: Is mosaic tiling hard to install?
mosaic-tiling.a: Mosaic tiling takes more time and patience than standard tiles because each small piece needs even spacing and pressure, but mesh-backed sheets make the process more manageable than loose individual pieces. Getting a level base and consistent grout lines is the trickiest part, so many homeowners still prefer to hire a qualified tiler.

reflective-foil-insulation.q: How much does reflective foil insulation cost in Australia?
reflective-foil-insulation.a: Reflective foil insulation installed in Australia typically costs $10 to $25 per square metre, similar to other insulation types. Material costs are a modest part of that figure since a single roll runs a few hundred dollars, so most of the price covers a professional correctly stapling, lapping, and taping the foil for it to perform properly.

reflective-foil-insulation.q: Does reflective foil insulation work in Australian climates?
reflective-foil-insulation.a: Reflective foil insulation works well in Australia because it reflects radiant heat, which is the main way heat moves through a roof space in hot climates, keeping the home cooler in summer. It performs best with an air gap on the reflective side and is often paired with bulk insulation for winter warmth too.

reflective-foil-insulation.q: Where is reflective foil insulation installed?
reflective-foil-insulation.a: Reflective foil insulation is most commonly installed under roof sheeting or rafters, facing down into the roof space, to block radiant heat before it reaches the ceiling. It can also line external walls during construction. It only works properly with a clear air gap left on the reflective side, so tight-packed installs lose most of the benefit.

roof-restoration.q: How much does roof restoration cost in Australia?
roof-restoration.a: Roof restoration in Australia typically costs $50 to $100 per hour for trade labour, and a full single-storey job usually runs into the thousands once several days of cleaning, priming, membrane coating, and repointing are included. Roof membrane costs around $249 per 15 litres and flexible pointing about $40 per 10 litres, with multiple batches needed for an average roof.

roof-restoration.q: How long does roof restoration take?
roof-restoration.a: A typical single-storey roof restoration takes two to five days, covering pressure cleaning, repairs, priming, and two coats of protective membrane with drying time between coats. Larger or steeper roofs, or those needing more repointing and ridge capping work, can take longer. Wet weather often delays the membrane coating stages specifically.

Roof restoration typically includes high-pressure cleaning, replacing broken or cracked tiles, repointing ridge capping with flexible pointing compound, priming, and applying two coats of protective membrane. It restores the look and waterproofing of an ageing roof without the cost of a full replacement, and usually comes with a workmanship warranty from the roofer.

steel-stud-framing.q: How much does steel stud framing cost in Australia?
steel-stud-framing.a: Steel stud framing in Australia typically costs $45 to $90 per hour for a licensed installer, since it is usually charged as part of a plastering or partition wall job rather than priced separately. A 64mm steel stud costs around $9 to $15 per 3-metre length, so a standard internal wall needs a modest material spend before labour.

steel-stud-framing.q: Is steel stud framing better than timber framing?
steel-stud-framing.a: Steel stud framing resists termites, warping, and shrinkage better than timber, and stays straighter over time, which suits bathrooms, commercial fit-outs, and tall partition walls. Timber framing is often cheaper, easier for tradespeople to modify on site, and remains the standard choice for most Australian house framing. The best option depends on the application.

steel-stud-framing.q: Can steel stud framing be used in load-bearing walls?
steel-stud-framing.a: Standard light-gauge steel studs are designed for non-load-bearing internal partitions, not structural load-bearing walls. Heavier structural steel framing systems can carry loads, but they need engineering design and different stud sizes and thicknesses than the 64mm studs used for typical internal walls. Always confirm the wall's structural role with your builder first.

vanity-installation.q: How much does vanity installation cost in Australia?
vanity-installation.a: Installing a new bathroom vanity in Australia typically costs $800 to $2,500 supply-and-installed, covering the vanity unit, tap, and a plumber's labour to disconnect and reconnect water and waste. Vanities themselves range from about $612 to $1,590 depending on size and finish, with mixer taps adding $93 to $326 on top.

vanity-installation.q: How deep is a vanity in Australia?
vanity-installation.a: Standard bathroom vanities in Australia are usually around 460mm to 465mm deep to fit comfortably in a typical bathroom without crowding the walkway. Slimline vanities as shallow as 350mm are available for tight ensuites, while some wall-hung and freestanding styles run deeper for extra storage. Always measure your space before ordering one.

vanity-installation.q: Can I install a bathroom vanity myself?
vanity-installation.a: Fitting a vanity cabinet in place is a manageable DIY task for a confident homeowner, but connecting the tap and waste to the water supply and drain should be left to a licensed plumber. Getting the plumbing done professionally protects your warranty and avoids leaks that can damage flooring and cabinetry over time.

balcony-waterproofing.q: How much does balcony waterproofing cost in Australia?
balcony-waterproofing.a: Balcony waterproofing costs $30 to $80 per square metre supplied and installed in Australia. A typical 10 square metre balcony runs roughly $300 to $800 depending on membrane type, access and how much of the existing surface needs stripping back before the waterproof membrane and reinforcing bandage go down.

balcony-waterproofing.q: What are the signs a balcony needs waterproofing?
balcony-waterproofing.a: Common warning signs include water stains or mould on the ceiling below the balcony, cracked or bubbling tiles, a spongy or discoloured surface, and water pooling instead of draining to the edge. Any of these point to a failed or ageing membrane and should be checked before internal damage sets in.

balcony-waterproofing.q: Can I waterproof a balcony myself?
balcony-waterproofing.a: Waterproofing a balcony yourself is risky in most of Australia because balcony and wet area waterproofing is licensed work in several states, and DIY jobs commonly fail at flashings, joints and drainage falls. A licensed waterproofer also provides a compliance certificate that insurers and future buyers will want to see.

ceiling-fan-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a ceiling fan in Australia?
ceiling-fan-installation.a: Ceiling fan installation in Australia typically costs $250 to $500 including the fan, based on an electrician's hourly rate of $70 to $130 plus a mid-range ceiling fan with light priced around $270. Costs rise if new wiring, a switch, or ceiling reinforcement is needed for a heavier fan.

ceiling-fan-installation.q: Can I install a ceiling fan myself?
ceiling-fan-installation.a: Wiring a ceiling fan into the mains yourself is illegal in Australia unless you hold an electrical licence, even though the fan itself is simple to mount. A licensed electrician needs to connect it to the switch circuit and confirm the ceiling can support the fan's weight and vibration safely.

ceiling-fan-installation.q: Do I need an electrician to install a ceiling fan?
ceiling-fan-installation.a: Yes, connecting a ceiling fan to household wiring is licensed electrical work in every Australian state, so a qualified electrician must handle the wiring and switch connection even if you buy and hang the fan yourself. This keeps the installation compliant and covered by warranty and insurance.

concrete-repair-and-crack-filling.q: How much does concrete crack repair cost in Australia?
concrete-repair-and-crack-filling.a: Concrete crack repair and patching typically costs $50 to $150 per square metre in Australia, depending on crack severity and surface prep. Small hairline cracks can sometimes be filled for the price of a bag of cement mix, from about $9 to $57, while wider structural cracks need a tradesperson.

Concrete cracks mainly from ground movement, shrinkage as it cures, tree root intrusion, poor drainage saturating the base, or inadequate reinforcing when it was originally poured. Reactive clay soils common across Australia make this worse, which is why cracks often reappear near driveways, paths and slab edges over time.

concrete-repair-and-crack-filling.q: Can I fill a concrete crack myself?
concrete-repair-and-crack-filling.a: Minor hairline cracks can be filled with a cement-based patching compound or crack filler from a hardware store, but wider or spreading cracks usually signal movement in the base and need a tradesperson to assess before repair. Sealing a crack without fixing the underlying cause often means it returns.

engineered-timber-flooring-installation.q: How much does engineered timber flooring cost to install in Australia?
engineered-timber-flooring-installation.a: Engineered timber flooring costs $160 to $250 per square metre installed in Australia, with the timber itself typically around $145 per square metre plus foam underlay at about $14 per square metre and laying labour on top. A 40 square metre living area generally lands between $6,400 and $10,000.

engineered-timber-flooring-installation.q: Is engineered timber flooring better than solid timber?
engineered-timber-flooring-installation.a: Engineered timber flooring is more dimensionally stable than solid timber because its layered plywood core resists expanding and contracting with humidity changes, making it suited to homes with underfloor heating or concrete slabs. Solid timber can be sanded and refinished more times over its life, but engineered boards install faster.

engineered-timber-flooring-installation.q: Can engineered timber flooring be installed over concrete?
engineered-timber-flooring-installation.a: Yes, engineered timber flooring can be glued or floated directly over a concrete slab once the slab is level, dry and tested for moisture. A foam underlay is typically used under a floating installation, and any low spots usually need a self-levelling compound first to stop the boards flexing or creaking.

frameless-shower-screen-installation.q: How much does a frameless shower screen cost in Australia?
frameless-shower-screen-installation.a: A frameless shower screen typically costs $900 to $2,200 supplied and installed in Australia, with the glass panel itself usually priced between $770 and $1,943 depending on size and hardware. Costs increase for larger screens, tinted or textured glass, and fixed panels over a walk-in opening.

frameless-shower-screen-installation.q: What are the disadvantages of a frameless shower screen?
frameless-shower-screen-installation.a: Frameless shower screens use thicker, heavier glass with no frame to catch water, so more water and steam can escape the shower area unless the glass and floor are sealed carefully with silicone. They also cost more upfront than framed or semi-frameless screens and are harder to replace if the glass is damaged.

frameless-shower-screen-installation.q: Do frameless shower screens need a frame at all?
frameless-shower-screen-installation.a: No, frameless shower screens rely on thick 10mm toughened glass, minimal clips and hinges, and a bead of sanitary silicone for support and waterproofing rather than an aluminium frame. This gives a cleaner look but means the glass and hardware need to be fitted precisely by a glazier to stay watertight.

home-rewiring.q: How much does it cost to rewire a house in Australia?
home-rewiring.a: Home rewiring in Australia is charged at an electrician's hourly rate of $70 to $130, since a full rewire is quoted as a project rather than a fixed figure. Cable alone runs about $499 per 100 metre roll, power points around $29 each, and a new switchboard from about $99, on top of labour.

home-rewiring.q: How long does it take to rewire a house?
home-rewiring.a: A full rewire of an average house typically takes an electrician several days to over a week, since every circuit needs to be run through walls and ceilings, tested and connected to a new or upgraded switchboard. Older homes with brick veneer, no roof access or asbestos sheeting can extend the job.

home-rewiring.q: Do I need a new switchboard when rewiring my house?
home-rewiring.a: Most home rewiring jobs include a switchboard upgrade, since old fuse-based boards cannot safely handle the safety switches and circuit breakers required under current wiring rules. A typical 8-way switchboard enclosure costs roughly $87 to $111, and pairing it with new safety switches is standard practice on a full rewire.

kitchen-splashback-installation.q: How much does a kitchen splashback cost to install in Australia?
kitchen-splashback-installation.a: A tiled kitchen splashback typically costs $60 to $180 per square metre supplied and installed, covering tiles priced from $14 to $59 per square metre plus adhesive and grout. A standard 4 to 6 square metre splashback often lands between $250 and $900 depending on the tile chosen.

kitchen-splashback-installation.q: What is the best material for a kitchen splashback?
kitchen-splashback-installation.a: Ceramic and porcelain tiles remain the most popular kitchen splashback material in Australia because they are affordable, heat resistant and easy to clean, with glass and stone splashbacks offering a seamless look at a higher price. The best choice depends on budget, grout preference and how hard the kitchen is used.

kitchen-splashback-installation.q: Can I install a kitchen splashback myself?
kitchen-splashback-installation.a: A ceramic tile splashback is one of the more DIY-friendly tiling jobs since it covers a small, flat, accessible area, but cutting around powerpoints, keeping lines straight and sealing edges properly trip up many first-time tilers. Professional installation adds a modest amount on top of material costs for a cleaner finish.

nbn-point-installation.q: How much does it cost to install an NBN point in Australia?
nbn-point-installation.a: Installing an extra NBN or data point in Australia typically costs $70 to $130 per hour for a licensed electrician or cabler, with a straightforward single point often taking under an hour once cabling is run. Cat6 cable itself costs about $8 to $40 per 305 metre box, so labour is the main cost.

nbn-point-installation.q: Who installs an NBN point, an electrician or NBN Co?
nbn-point-installation.a: NBN Co only installs the connection box at the boundary or wall where the network first enters the home, not extra internal data points. Adding a new NBN or network point elsewhere in the house is done by a licensed electrician or data cabler, separate from the initial NBN Co connection.

nbn-point-installation.q: Can I install an NBN point myself?
nbn-point-installation.a: Running and terminating structured cabling for a new NBN or network point is licensed cabling work in Australia, so it cannot legally be done by an unlicensed homeowner beyond basic patch leads. A licensed technician also tests the finished cable run to confirm it meets Cat6 performance standards before use.

render-crack-repair.q: How much does render crack repair cost in Australia?
render-crack-repair.a: Render crack repair typically costs $30 to $80 per square metre in Australia, depending on crack width and how much surrounding render needs cutting back. Small hairline cracks can sometimes be patched with a flexible gap filler from around $6 to $23 a cartridge, while wider cracks need a render mix and a tradesperson.

Render cracks mainly from building movement, shrinkage as the render cures, moisture getting behind the surface, or render applied too thick over a poorly prepared wall. Hairline cracking is common and often cosmetic, but wider or spreading cracks can let water into the wall and should be checked promptly.

render-crack-repair.q: Can I repair render cracks myself?
render-crack-repair.a: Small hairline cracks can be filled with a flexible exterior gap filler as a temporary fix, but matching the texture and colour of existing render is difficult without the right tools and mix ratio. For a durable, near-invisible repair, especially on wider cracks, a rendering tradesperson gets a better long-term result.

security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.q: How much does it cost to install CCTV cameras in Australia?
security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.a: CCTV installation in Australia typically costs $70 to $130 per hour for a licensed electrician, with a 4-camera kit priced from about $89 to $399 depending on resolution and features. A standard home system with wiring and setup often totals a few hundred to over a thousand dollars depending on camera count.

security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.q: Do I need an electrician to install security cameras?
security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.a: Wireless battery or Wi-Fi cameras can usually be mounted without an electrician, but wired CCTV systems that run cable back to a recorder or need extra power points should be installed by a licensed electrician or data cabler. This keeps the wiring compliant and avoids exposed cable runs around the house.

security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.q: Where should security cameras be placed on a house?
security-camera-and-cctv-wiring.a: Cameras are generally placed covering the front door, driveway, back entry and any side access points hidden from the street, mounted high enough to avoid tampering but low enough to capture faces clearly. Avoid pointing cameras directly into strong backlight like a rising or setting sun, which washes out footage.

stone-benchtop-installation.q: How much does a stone benchtop cost in Australia?
stone-benchtop-installation.a: A stone benchtop typically costs $800 to $1,320 per square metre supplied in Australia, plus fabrication and fitting by a stonemason. An average kitchen benchtop of around 5 square metres often lands between $4,800 and $7,500 installed, once edge profiling and cutouts for sinks and cooktops are added.

stone-benchtop-installation.q: Is engineered stone still allowed in Australia?
stone-benchtop-installation.a: No, working with engineered stone benchtops was banned nationally from 1 July 2024 due to the silicosis risk from cutting and polishing the material. Tradespeople can no longer fabricate or install new engineered stone benchtops, so homeowners now choose porcelain, natural stone or laminate for new kitchens instead.

stone-benchtop-installation.q: What can I use instead of engineered stone for a benchtop?
stone-benchtop-installation.a: Since engineered stone was banned in Australia from 1 July 2024, popular alternatives include porcelain benchtops, which resist heat and scratches well, and natural stone like granite or marble, both priced in a similar range to what engineered stone previously cost. Laminate remains the budget option for tighter renovations.

vinyl-plank-installation.q: How much does vinyl plank flooring cost to install in Australia?
vinyl-plank-installation.a: Vinyl plank flooring costs $40 to $150 per square metre installed in Australia, with the planks themselves typically priced between $25 and $64 per square metre depending on thickness and finish. A 30 square metre living area generally costs $1,200 to $4,500 fitted, with extra for levelling an uneven subfloor.

Most rigid vinyl plank flooring sold in Australia is fully waterproof at the board level, built with a solid core rather than the fibreboard core used in laminate, so it handles spills and damp areas like kitchens and laundries well. The seams and edges still need correct installation to stop water tracking underneath.

vinyl-plank-installation.q: Does vinyl plank flooring need underlay?
vinyl-plank-installation.a: Vinyl plank flooring often includes an attached foam or cork backing, but a separate underlay is still recommended over concrete or uneven timber subfloors for extra sound dampening and comfort underfoot. Any dips or high spots in the subfloor usually need a self-levelling compound before the planks go down.

bamboo-flooring-installation.q: How much does bamboo flooring installation cost in Australia?
bamboo-flooring-installation.a: Bamboo flooring installation in Australia typically costs $40–$150 per square metre supply and install, depending on flooring grade and subfloor prep. Foam underlay adds around $14 per square metre. A 40m² room installation typically lands between $1,600 and $6,000 including materials and labour. Get a few quotes to compare like for like.

bamboo-flooring-installation.q: Is bamboo flooring a good option for Australian homes?
bamboo-flooring-installation.a: Bamboo flooring suits most Australian homes, offering hardwood looks at a lower price with good scratch resistance. It performs best in stable indoor climates since it can expand or contract with humidity swings, so coastal and tropical homes need acclimatised, quality-grade boards. Avoid areas with standing water like bathrooms and laundries.

bamboo-flooring-installation.q: Does bamboo flooring need an underlay?
bamboo-flooring-installation.a: Yes, bamboo flooring should go over a foam underlay, which costs around $14 per square metre at Bunnings. Underlay cushions the boards, reduces footstep noise, and evens out minor subfloor imperfections. On concrete slabs a moisture barrier layer is also recommended before laying, since bamboo is sensitive to rising damp.

ceiling-insulation-installation.q: How much does ceiling insulation installation cost in Australia?
ceiling-insulation-installation.a: Ceiling insulation installation in Australia costs $10–$25 per square metre supply and install. R4.0 batts run $61–$124 a pack at Bunnings, with coverage varying by product thickness. For an average 150m² home this typically totals $1,500–$3,750 for a full ceiling cavity installed by a licensed installer.

ceiling-insulation-installation.q: What R-value ceiling insulation is recommended in Australia?
ceiling-insulation-installation.a: Most Australian homes use R4.0 batts in the ceiling, which suit most climate zones for comfortable year-round performance. Cooler regions typically benefit from a higher R-value, while warmer northern areas can get by with slightly less. A qualified insulation installer can confirm the right rating for your roof space and location before you buy.

ceiling-insulation-installation.q: How long does ceiling insulation take to install?
ceiling-insulation-installation.a: Ceiling insulation installation typically takes half a day to a full day for an average home, depending on roof access and cavity size. Installers lay batts between and over the ceiling joists from inside the roof space. Homes with restricted roof access or existing insulation needing removal can take longer.

concrete-retaining-wall.q: How much does a concrete retaining wall cost in Australia?
concrete-retaining-wall.a: A concrete retaining wall in Australia typically costs $50–$150 per square metre supply and install, depending on wall height, reinforcement, and site access. Reinforcing bar and formwork add to material costs, and drainage behind the wall is essential. A modest 10m² wall usually falls between $500 and $1,500.

concrete-retaining-wall.q: Does a concrete retaining wall need drainage?
concrete-retaining-wall.a: Yes, every concrete retaining wall needs drainage behind it to relieve water pressure that can crack or push over the wall. Standard practice uses slotted ag pipe wrapped in drainage gravel, running along the base and out to a discharge point. Skipping drainage is one of the most common causes of retaining wall failure.

concrete-retaining-wall.q: How thick should a concrete retaining wall be?
concrete-retaining-wall.a: Wall thickness depends on height and the soil load behind it, but most residential concrete retaining walls under one metre use around 150–200mm of reinforced concrete. Taller walls need thicker sections, deeper footings, and engineered reinforcement with N12 bar. Always get a structural design for anything retaining significant soil height.

epoxy-flooring.q: How much does epoxy flooring cost in Australia?
epoxy-flooring.a: Epoxy flooring in Australia costs $40–$150 per square metre supply and install, depending on the number of coats and surface prep needed. A DIY epoxy coating kit runs $53–$198 at Bunnings, cheaper but harder to get a durable finish. Professional installers grind and prime the concrete first for proper adhesion.

epoxy-flooring.q: What are the downsides of epoxy flooring?
epoxy-flooring.a: Epoxy flooring can be slippery when wet unless an anti-slip additive is mixed in, and it shows scratches and yellowing over time with UV exposure. It also needs a well-prepped, dry concrete slab, since moisture underneath causes bubbling and peeling. Repairs mean patching or recoating rather than simple spot fixes.

epoxy-flooring.q: What surfaces can epoxy flooring not be applied to?
epoxy-flooring.a: Epoxy will not bond well to sealed or waxed concrete, damp slabs, or flexible surfaces like vinyl and some timber, since it needs a porous, mechanically ground surface to key into. It also struggles on surfaces contaminated with oil or grease. A professional will grind and test the slab before quoting a job.

french-drain-installation.q: How much does a French drain cost to install in Australia?
french-drain-installation.a: A French drain installation in Australia typically costs $300–$2,000 per job, depending on length, depth, and ground conditions. Materials like slotted ag pipe and drainage gravel are inexpensive, so most of the cost is labour for digging the trench and correctly grading the fall. Longer runs across a whole yard sit at the higher end.

french-drain-installation.q: What is a French drain used for?
french-drain-installation.a: A French drain is a gravel-filled trench with a slotted or perforated pipe underneath that redirects groundwater away from a house, retaining wall, or waterlogged garden bed. It works by letting water seep through the gravel into the pipe, then carries it to a discharge point or stormwater connection. It is a common fix for soggy yards and damp foundations.

french-drain-installation.q: How deep should a French drain be?
french-drain-installation.a: Most residential French drains sit around 300 to 600mm deep, enough to intercept groundwater above the footing line without undermining it. Depth also depends on what the drain is protecting, with retaining walls often needing a deeper trench than a simple garden drainage line. A tradesperson will grade the trench with a slight fall toward the outlet.

hot-water-system-replacement.q: How much does it cost to replace a hot water system in Australia?
hot-water-system-replacement.a: Replacing a hot water system in Australia typically costs $80–$200 per hour in plumber labour, plus the unit itself. An electric storage hot water system costs $98–$528 depending on tank size and brand, so a straightforward swap often lands between $600 and $1,500 including installation. Gas or heat pump units cost more upfront.

hot-water-system-replacement.q: How long does a hot water system last?
hot-water-system-replacement.a: Most electric storage hot water systems last around 8 to 12 years, while gas and heat pump units can run a bit longer with regular servicing. Signs it needs replacing include rusty water, rumbling noises, or leaks around the base of the tank. Replacing before a full failure avoids water damage and an unplanned cold shower.

hot-water-system-replacement.q: How long does it take to replace a hot water system?
hot-water-system-replacement.a: A straightforward like-for-like hot water system replacement usually takes a licensed plumber 2 to 4 hours, including draining the old tank and connecting the new one. Switching between fuel types, such as electric to gas, takes longer due to extra pipework and compliance checks. Most homes are back to hot water the same day.

kitchen-splashback-tiling.q: How much does a kitchen splashback cost to tile in Australia?
kitchen-splashback-tiling.a: A tiled kitchen splashback in Australia typically costs $45–$120 per square metre supply and install. Ceramic wall tiles run $14–$59 per square metre, plus adhesive and grout, so a standard 3 to 4 square metre splashback often totals $200–$500 in materials before labour. Mosaic or feature tiles push the price toward the higher end.

kitchen-splashback-tiling.q: What is the best tile for a kitchen splashback?
kitchen-splashback-tiling.a: Ceramic and porcelain tiles are the most popular kitchen splashback choice in Australia, since they resist heat, grease, and staining while being easy to wipe clean. Glass and mosaic tiles suit a feature look but cost more and can be trickier to grout cleanly around powerpoints and rangehoods. Gloss finishes brighten a kitchen and make cleaning easier.

kitchen-splashback-tiling.q: How long does it take to tile a kitchen splashback?
kitchen-splashback-tiling.a: Tiling a standard kitchen splashback usually takes a tiler one day, covering measuring, cutting around powerpoints, laying tiles, and grouting once the adhesive has set. Larger or more intricate patterns, like herringbone or mosaic, can take an extra day. Allow another day before the grout fully cures if you plan to use the stovetop straight away.

paving-and-pathways.q: How much does paving cost per square metre in Australia?
paving-and-pathways.a: Paving in Australia typically costs $50–$150 per square metre supply and install, depending on paver type and base preparation. Concrete pavers cost around $15 each at Bunnings, with paving sand and crusher dust adding to the base cost. A basic 20m² pathway usually runs $1,000–$3,000 including labour.

paving-and-pathways.q: What is the cheapest type of paving?
paving-and-pathways.a: Concrete pavers are generally the cheapest paving option in Australia, costing around $15 each compared with natural stone options like bluestone or travertine, which run well above $100 per square metre. Crushed gravel or crusher dust paths cost even less but are not as durable or level underfoot. Concrete still gives a clean, long-lasting finish for the price.

Laying pavers yourself is possible for a small, flat area like a garden path, but getting the base compacted and level takes practice. Professional pavers excavate, compact a road base or crusher dust layer, then bed pavers in sand with consistent joints and fall for drainage. Skipping proper base prep is the main reason DIY paving sinks or cracks later.

render-repair.q: How much does render repair cost in Australia?
render-repair.a: Render repair in Australia typically costs $30–$80 per square metre, covering crack filling, patching, and reblending the finish to match existing render. Polymer render mix costs around $15 per 20kg bag at Bunnings for small DIY patches. Larger areas of cracking or delamination cost more, since loose render often needs to be hacked off before repair.

Render cracks mainly from movement in the building, moisture getting behind the render, or render that was applied too thick or over a poorly prepared surface. Hairline cracks are usually cosmetic, but wider or spreading cracks can let water in and damage the wall behind. Fixing the underlying cause matters as much as patching the crack itself.

render-repair.q: Can you patch render or does the whole wall need redoing?
render-repair.a: Small cracks and localised damage can usually be patched without redoing the whole wall, provided the surrounding render is sound and well bonded. If render is bulging, hollow-sounding when tapped, or crumbling over a large area, it usually needs to be removed and reapplied in that section. A tradesperson can tell the difference with a simple tap test.

sewer-line-replacement.q: How much does sewer line replacement cost in Australia?
sewer-line-replacement.a: Sewer line replacement in Australia typically costs $80–$200 per hour in plumber labour, with the total heavily dependent on pipe length, depth, and whether trenchless relining is used instead of full excavation. PVC pipe itself is cheap at $6–$32 per length, so labour and access dominate the final price.

sewer-line-replacement.q: What are the signs a sewer line needs replacing?
sewer-line-replacement.a: Common signs include recurring blockages, gurgling drains, sewage smells in the yard, wet or sunken patches over the pipe run, and toilets that drain slowly despite clearing. Tree root intrusion and old clay or earthenware pipes are frequent culprits in older homes. A camera inspection confirms whether the line needs relining or full replacement.

sewer-line-replacement.q: Do I need to dig up my yard to replace a sewer line?
sewer-line-replacement.a: Not always. Trenchless relining can rehabilitate a damaged sewer pipe through small access points, avoiding a full dig-up in many cases. It works best on pipes that are cracked or root-affected but still structurally intact. Severely collapsed or misaligned sections usually still need traditional excavation to replace the pipe properly.

stormwater-drainage-installation.q: How much does stormwater drainage installation cost in Australia?
stormwater-drainage-installation.a: Stormwater drainage installation in Australia typically costs $300–$2,000 per job, depending on pipe length, number of pits, and how much excavation is needed. A grated drainage pit costs $41–$108 each, with PVC stormwater pipe adding $6–$26 per length. Connecting into council stormwater infrastructure or dealing with tree roots can push costs higher.

stormwater-drainage-installation.q: What is the difference between stormwater and regular drainage?
stormwater-drainage-installation.a: Stormwater drainage specifically manages rainwater runoff from roofs, driveways, and paved areas, carrying it away through pipes and pits to the street system or a legal point of discharge. General site drainage, like a French drain, deals with groundwater or subsurface moisture around footings and gardens. The two systems often connect but serve different jobs.

stormwater-drainage-installation.q: Why is proper stormwater drainage important?
stormwater-drainage-installation.a: Poor stormwater drainage lets water pool against foundations, erode garden beds, and flood low points in the yard during heavy rain, which over time can cause structural and damp problems. A properly graded system with pits and piped connections moves runoff away from the house to a legal discharge point, protecting the property long term.

wall-hung-vanity-installation.q: How much does it cost to install a wall-hung vanity in Australia?
wall-hung-vanity-installation.a: A wall-hung vanity unit costs $451–$1,999 in Australia, with $1,102 typical for a quality 900mm unit, plus $93–$326 for a basin mixer tap. Installed as a standalone swap by a plumber, labour typically adds a few hundred dollars on top. As part of a full bathroom renovation, overall project costs commonly run from $15,000–$35,000.

wall-hung-vanity-installation.q: Why choose a wall-hung vanity over a floor-standing one?
wall-hung-vanity-installation.a: A wall-hung vanity makes a small bathroom feel larger by leaving the floor visible underneath, and it makes mopping and cleaning easier since there is nothing blocking the skirting. It also suits modern, minimalist bathroom designs. The trade-off is it needs solid wall reinforcement, since the cabinet and any stored items hang entirely off brackets fixed into the studs.

wall-hung-vanity-installation.q: Does a wall need extra support for a wall-hung vanity?
wall-hung-vanity-installation.a: Yes, a wall-hung vanity needs solid backing, usually a plywood or timber noggin fitted between the wall studs, to carry the weight of the cabinet, benchtop, and basin. Standard plasterboard alone will not hold the brackets long term. This backing is normally installed during a renovation before the wall is sheeted and tiled, so it pays to plan ahead.

bath-to-shower-conversion.q: How much does a bath to shower conversion cost in Australia?
bath-to-shower-conversion.a: A bath to shower conversion typically costs $15,000 to $35,000 in Australia when done as part of a full bathroom renovation, covering waterproofing, tiling and a new screen. A semi-frameless shower screen alone runs $275 to $1,008, with a 15L waterproofing membrane adding roughly $59 to $262 to the job.

bath-to-shower-conversion.q: What does converting a bath to a shower involve?
bath-to-shower-conversion.a: Converting a bath to a shower involves removing the old bath, re-waterproofing the wet area with a membrane, then tiling the floor and often the walls before fitting a new shower screen and shower head. Porcelain floor tiles typically cost $28.90 to $125 per square metre, with tile adhesive around $15 to $62 a bag.

bath-to-shower-conversion.q: Can a bath to shower conversion work in a small bathroom?
bath-to-shower-conversion.a: Yes, a bath to shower conversion often suits a small bathroom better than keeping the bath, since a shower stall needs less floor space. It frees up room for a larger vanity or extra storage, and a semi-frameless screen from around $359 keeps the footprint compact without cutting into the room.

ceiling-painting.q: How much does ceiling painting cost in Australia?
ceiling-painting.a: Ceiling painting in Australia typically costs $40 to $70 per hour for a professional painter, with most single rooms taking half a day to complete. A 10L tin of ceiling paint costs around $57, and a roller and tray kit adds a further $3 to $12 to the job.

ceiling-painting.q: What is the cheapest way to paint a ceiling?
ceiling-painting.a: The cheapest way to paint a ceiling is to buy a budget ceiling paint from around $33 for 10 litres, use a basic roller and tray kit costing as little as $3, and do the rolling yourself, only hiring a painter for high or angled ceilings that need scaffolding or extra care.

ceiling-painting.q: How many coats of paint does a ceiling need?
ceiling-painting.a: Most ceilings need two coats of ceiling paint for even, streak-free coverage, especially when covering a darker colour or water stains. A single 10L tin, priced around $57, generally covers one coat over an average room, so budget for a second tin if the ceiling needs full coverage.

deck-balustrade-installation.q: How much does deck balustrade installation cost in Australia?
deck-balustrade-installation.a: Deck balustrade installation in Australia is usually quoted within the broader $200 to $1,000 per square metre decking trade range, since balustrades are typically priced as part of the deck build. Stainless wire balustrade hardware kits cost around $7 to $32, plus treated pine framing at $5 to $23 per metre.

deck-balustrade-installation.q: What is a deck balustrade for?
deck-balustrade-installation.a: A deck balustrade is a safety barrier fitted along the open edges of a raised deck to stop people falling off, and it is required on most elevated decks in Australia. Common materials include stainless wire cable, glass panels, timber and aluminium, chosen to suit the deck's style and budget.

deck-balustrade-installation.q: What materials are deck balustrades made from?
deck-balustrade-installation.a: Deck balustrades are commonly built from stainless wire cable strung between posts, framed timber palings, glass panels for an open view, or powder-coated aluminium. A stainless wire balustrade kit costs roughly $7 to $32, while treated pine framing runs about $5 to $23 per linear metre.

ev-charger-installation.q: How much does EV charger installation cost in Australia?
ev-charger-installation.a: EV charger installation in Australia typically costs $3,300 to $8,000 fully installed, covering the electrician's labour, cabling and any switchboard work. The charger unit itself is far cheaper, from $162 to $799 (around $285 typical for a 7kW single-phase model), with the rest covering wiring and safety compliance.

ev-charger-installation.q: Can an EV charger be plugged into a normal power point?
ev-charger-installation.a: No, an EV charger should not run off a standard power point long term. It needs a dedicated circuit wired directly to the switchboard with its own safety switch (RCBO), since EV charging draws a sustained high current that a regular household socket and cabling are not rated for.

ev-charger-installation.q: Does installing an EV charger require a switchboard upgrade?
ev-charger-installation.a: Sometimes. Many homes need a new circuit added to the switchboard with a dedicated safety switch, typically $14 to $40 per RCBO, plus heavier cabling run from the board to the charger. Older switchboards with limited capacity may need a fuller upgrade before an EV charger can be added safely.

garden-bed-construction.q: How much does garden bed construction cost in Australia?
garden-bed-construction.a: Garden bed construction in Australia typically costs $50 to $150 per square metre installed. Garden soil runs about $6 to $22 for a 25L bag, hardwood mulch $11 to $20 for 60L, and steel edging to define the bed's border costs roughly $14 to $44 per metre.

garden-bed-construction.q: What is the cheapest way to build a garden bed?
garden-bed-construction.a: The cheapest way to build a garden bed is to skip retaining blocks and use steel edging from around $14 per metre to define the border, fill with budget garden soil from about $6 a bag, then top with mulch to suppress weeds instead of paying for a weed mat.

garden-bed-construction.q: What goes at the bottom of a raised garden bed?
garden-bed-construction.a: A layer of weed mat is usually laid at the bottom of a raised garden bed to stop weeds and grass growing up through the soil, costing roughly $24 to $80 per roll. Garden soil and a layer of mulch on top complete the bed and help retain moisture.

house-painting.q: How much does house painting cost in Australia?
house-painting.a: House painting in Australia typically costs $40 to $70 per hour for a professional painter, with total project cost scaling with the size of the house and number of coats. Exterior acrylic paint runs about $28 to $109 for 10 litres, and interior low-sheen paint around $50 to $254.

house-painting.q: Do you need to prime before painting a house?
house-painting.a: Yes, priming is generally recommended before painting a house, especially over bare timber, previously unpainted surfaces or patched areas, since it helps the topcoat bond evenly and cover consistently. A 10L primer sealer undercoat costs around $48 to $186, depending on the surface and coverage needed.

house-painting.q: How many coats of paint does a house need?
house-painting.a: Most house painting jobs use a primer coat followed by two topcoats for full, even coverage, particularly when changing colour or covering stains. Skipping to a single topcoat over an unprimed surface often leaves patchy results, so budgeting for primer plus two coats gives the most reliable finish.

laminate-flooring-installation.q: How much does laminate flooring installation cost in Australia?
laminate-flooring-installation.a: Laminate flooring installation in Australia typically costs $40 to $150 per square metre, professionally fitted. The laminate boards themselves cost $19 to $64 per square metre, around $43 typical, plus a foam underlay at about $14 per square metre to cushion the floor and reduce noise.

laminate-flooring-installation.q: What's better, vinyl or laminate flooring?
laminate-flooring-installation.a: Vinyl handles moisture better and suits bathrooms, laundries and kitchens, while laminate gives a harder, more realistic timber look for living areas and bedrooms but is less water-tolerant. Neither is universally better; the right choice comes down to the room, foot traffic and how much water exposure it gets.
